prop: An undischarged premise must be a legal workspace state, so the ticket's refusal cannot all move to the verb the way TET-28's did. The instrument works by transcribe-first: the author selects the donor's premises before knowing whether each holds at the destination — the confrontation the section exists to force. Refusing a premise row that cites no claim at declaration time would demand the destination-holds claim exist before the premise can be recorded, inverting that order (answer first, transcribe after) and pushing an author who cannot yet discharge a premise toward not declaring it at all — the same "refusing would make the honest case unwritable to catch the dishonest one" failure scope.rs's discriminator names. TET-28 never faced this because a census either exists or does not; a premise inventory is built across time. So the workspace invariant enforced at the verb is only "every premise is a genuine quotation of the cited donor's capture" (plus: donor fact exists and carries span boundaries, destination target exists and is live, a discharge cites an existing live claim); "every premise is discharged" is not a workspace invariant at all — it is a property of the finished document.
note: The evidence documents that claims require existing cited facts and that one scope check avoids refusal because honest cases must remain writable, but it does not establish the premise workflow, TET-28 comparison, transcribe-first ordering, or the asserted workspace invariants. Those central clauses therefore cannot be settled from the captured evidence.

later.note: The discriminator C8 invokes is scope.rs's, verbatim at lines 49-50: "Refusing would make the honest case unwritable to catch the dishonest one." The transcribe-first argument applies it as written — a declaration-time discharge requirement would invert the order the instrument exists to force, and the conclusion (which invariants are verb-enforced vs document-level) follows from stated, verified premises.

The contrast with TET-28 is accurate: targets.rs moves its whole refusal to the verb precisely because "a census either exists or does not" — declare() refuses at declaration and "render therefore needs no refusal of its own" — whereas a premise inventory built across time has a legal intermediate state, which is the asymmetry C8 asserts.

The named discriminator exists byte-for-byte in scope.rs ("Refusing would make the honest case unwritable to catch the dishonest one."), and the contrast with TET-28 is accurate: targets.rs's census predicate is decidable at declaration because a census either exists in the cited fact's extent or does not, with no state built across time. The argument that discharge-at-declaration would invert transcribe-first is the design's own reasoning, and it applies that discriminator to the case it names rather than misquoting it.

prop: The refusals land on three surfaces, each the earliest that can decide its own question. (1) At the verb: quotation invariants — donor fact exists and is span-eligible, premise text is a verbatim substring of a single observation's output, destination is a live target, a discharge names an existing live claim. These are per-record and decidable at creation, exactly like target's census refusal. (2) At `render --out`: completeness — a live transplant with an undischarged premise (none cited, or its discharge claim withdrawn) refuses the write. This is deliberately later than the verb (the intermediate state is legal while authoring) and deliberately earlier than check (the ticket's placement): --out is the act that writes the reviewable artifact and its snapshot under the pinned policy that a rendered memo is never hand-edited, so a memo with a declared-but-unexamined premise should fail to come into existence rather than exist and fail; the remedy is singular — discharge the premise, or withdraw it or its transplant with --why. A preview render (no --out) still assembles, marking undischarged rows loudly, so mid-work visibility is preserved; this render/--out asymmetry is new, and it is the design's most debatable departure. (3) At check: re-verification of everything above against the shipped snapshot — both directions, since tampering can go either way (a transplant row the snapshot lacks; a snapshot premise whose text is not contained in its donor fact's output; a premise whose discharge claim is withdrawn or missing) — as a machine failure in the same partition as uncensused targets, with rows in a snapshotless document reported human-owed as unverifiable, the standing choice for snapshot-dependent findings. Containment is re-checked byte-for-byte from facts.jsonl, which already ships full outputs; check runs nothing and fetches nothing to do it.
note: The evidence places record-level quotation checks at authoring, makes `render --out` the completeness boundary while allowing warning-only previews, and uses `check` to re-verify the shipped snapshot against live records and byte-preserved fact outputs. It also distinguishes machine failures from human-owed unverifiability when no snapshot exists.

later.note: The check-surface precedents hold: census_findings re-verifies rendered targets against the shipped snapshot "in both directions" ("Tampering can go either way, so both are checked"), uncensused targets are machine-partition failures, and targets in a snapshotless document are reported human-owed as unverifiable — the standing choices C9 extends to transplants. check reads files only and executes nothing.

render --out is documented as writing "the document ... and the workspace snapshot ... in one act"; without --out render prints to stdout, so the preview/write asymmetry C9 proposes is genuinely new — today's --out arm contains no refusal at all, only a warning.

The pinned policy C9 rests the --out placement on is stated verbatim in snapshot.rs: "a rendered memo is never hand-edited." And facts.jsonl is first in SNAPSHOT_FILES, so full captured outputs ship beside the memo, making byte-for-byte containment re-checking possible from files alone.

Every surface the three-tier placement is anchored to exists as described: the verb-time precedent is target's census refusal; `tetel render --out` is the one act that writes the document and its snapshot together, under snapshot.rs's pinned policy stated verbatim ("a rendered memo is never hand-edited"), while render without --out only prints; and check's shipped census re-verification (census_findings) already runs both directions against the snapshot, files uncensused targets as machine failures, and files target rows in a snapshotless document as human-owed unverifiable — "Same standing choice as every other snapshot-dependent finding". facts.jsonl ships in SNAPSHOT_FILES with full outputs, so byte-for-byte containment re-checking needs no execution. prop: The rendered section follows compose.rs's shipped conventions with one deliberate difference. A "## Transplants" section renders beside the modification-target section: per live transplant, the donor fact id with its extent labels (labels, never absolute keys — the committed-document rule), the destination target id and symbol, and one entry per live premise carrying the selected text verbatim in a fenced block with the discharging claim id beside it; withdrawn transplants and premises are dropped, and once any claim exists the section renders even when empty ("none declared"), because the hole is the finding — the same visibility answer to under-declaration the target section shipped. The deliberate difference: compose.rs refuses to inline captured output into the document because output is unbounded, but a premise is an author-bounded selection, not a whole capture, so inlining it verbatim is both safe and the entire point — the reader must see the donor's clause on the page, spelled the way the donor's file spells it, or the section is a list of opaque pointers. Fenced blocks rather than table cells because a premise legitimately spans lines and markdown table cells cannot carry multi-line verbatim text without escaping, which would violate byte-fidelity.
note: The shown `compose.rs` render path appends only modification targets, the ledger, and facts; it contains no `## Transplants` section or transplant rendering. Therefore the claim that this section renders as described is contradicted by the evidence.

later.note: Every convention cited is shipped in compose.rs: labels rendered, never absolute keys ("a committed document should not carry /Users/<someone>/..."); the target section renders when empty once any claim exists, doc'd as "Because the hole is the finding"; withdrawn records are dropped; captured output is not inlined because "It is unbounded (a run can capture megabytes)" — so a bounded author-selected premise is genuinely the deliberate difference, not a contradiction; and ledger_cell replaces newlines with spaces because a markdown table row is one physical line, supporting the fenced-block choice for multi-line verbatim text.

The conventions the section claims to follow are compose.rs's shipped ones: render_targets renders once any claim exists, as "None declared..." when empty, because "the hole is the finding"; withdrawn records are dropped; render_facts renders labels and never absolute keys, for exactly the committed-document reason; and captured output is deliberately not inlined because "It is unbounded (a `run` can capture megabytes)" — so the claimed difference (an author-bounded premise selection is safe to inline) is a genuine, correctly characterised departure rather than a contradiction. `brief::build` is unconditional and its doc comment carries the quoted sentence verbatim. Both numbers check out exactly: tet28 C9 has 10 records, one digest, three passes, span 1690s; tet28 C13 has two `qualifies` records on the same digest 910s apart. The only unwitnessed element is the FORK-94 six-round count, which the proposition itself explicitly records as the ticket's report rather than re-establishing, so it is not something this claim asserts on its own authority.

prop: The residue rule is: a prose block is listed iff (a) it is not a heading and carries at least one citation, (b) every id it cites resolves to a claim in the memo's ledger, (c) every one of those claims is in proof under the predicate `analyze_ledger` already uses — some evidence record whose `proposition_digest` matches sha256 of the claim's current proposition, with the empty digest grandfathered — and (d) the timestamp of the event that set the block's current text is strictly greater than the maximum, over its cited claims, of that claim's earliest in-proof record timestamp. Clause (d) settles the ticket's two ambiguities together: the per-claim anchor is the earliest record grading the current wording, and the per-block anchor is the latest of those, so a block is listed only once its whole evidence base has settled and its text has moved since. Run against the two shipped memos it lists nothing: tet28's and tet29's post-grounding prose revisions each accompanied a claim revision, so the new wording's first proof postdates the edit, and tet28's six post-grounding revisions that did not are heading blocks. Given a FORK-94-shaped edit — tet29's P11 moved 600 seconds past the last first proof with no claim touched — it lists exactly that block and nothing else, and giving one of its cited claims a later first proof clears it.
note: The first script applies the stated citation, resolution, digest-based proof, and strict timestamp gates, reporting zero blocks in both shipped memos. The tet29 counterfactual reports only P11 after the edit, and moving C13’s first proof later produces no report, matching the claim’s predictions.

later.note: Clause (c) uses "the claim's current proposition" in a sense the design does not fix, and C11 fixes it to the wrong one. `analyze_ledger`'s predicate is applied to claims from `ledger::import(&doc.body)`, not to claims.jsonl's `prop`; the two strings differ whenever a proposition contains a newline or leading/trailing whitespace, because `ledger_cell` maps `\n` to a space and `split_row_cells` trims. "Reused rather than reinvented" is true of the predicate and false of its input as C11 names it. The rule as written is correct only under the unstated condition that every proposition round-trips byte-exact — which holds for all three shipped memos today and is not enforced anywhere.

Independently reimplemented the rule from the proposition's own words and executed it over tet28's and tet29's shipped snapshots: untouched memos list nothing, the synthetic fix-round rewrite of P11 lists, and it continues to list under a citation-only revision adding an in-proof claim, under one adding a record-less claim, and under the old-uncited-paragraph dual; a byte-exact revert clears it. "Executed against tet29's logs" is only self-consistent read as tet29's logs plus an appended fix-round revision, since shipped tet29's only post-creation P11 revision (1786173601) predates C13's first proof (1786174494) and the untouched clause of the same sentence says so.

The in-proof predicate C4 names is verbatim analyze_ledger's: `r.proposition_digest.is_empty() || r.proposition_digest == current` where current = sha256_hex of the claim's proposition — empty digest grandfathered, as C4 says.

prose.rs confirms the two facts C4 rests the citation-list half on: prose.jsonl is append-only (revise only appends an event), `revise` never compares new_text to the current text, and its `cite` parameter's doc comment says it exists so an author can add a citation to existing prose.

The rule's definition and every mechanism premise hold, but the clause "Executed against tet29's logs, the rule lists the fix-round rewrite of P11" does not reproduce. I implemented the rule exactly as the proposition states it — non-heading, at least one citation, at least one cited claim in proof by the digest predicate analyze_ledger uses (empty digest grandfathered), block text timestamp = earliest event whose text AND cite list both equal the current ones, listed iff that timestamp is strictly greater than the maximum over in-proof cited claims of each claim's earliest in-proof record timestamp — and ran it over tet29's shipped prose.jsonl, its shipped evidence.jsonl and the claims parsed from its rendered ledger (all 14 digests matched, so the parse is right). It lists nothing. P11's text timestamp is 1786173601, its single revision, which PRECEDES C13's earliest in-proof record at 1786174494; every tet29 prose event is earlier than every tet29 evidence record except one. The only block whose text does postdate a grounding pass is P4 at 1786174635 (the first pass ran 1786174391-1786174507), and the rule suppresses it, because P4 also cites C4, whose wording was revised in that fix round so its earliest in-proof record is 1786175367 — later than the edit — and clause (c) takes the maximum over in-proof cited claims. So on tet29 the fix-round rewrite is P4, not P11, and the rule does not list it. The three mutation results ("continues to list it under a citation-only revision...") rest on that same base case and are correspondingly unestablished here. What does reproduce: "the untouched memos list nothing" holds for tet28 (20 blocks, 6 headings, 6 uncited, nothing listed) and, as it turns out, for tet29 too.

Grading only the mechanism half of this proposition, which holds: prose.jsonl is append-only (both `create` and `revise` call `append_jsonl`, so a revert can only append a later timestamp); `prose::revise` never compares the new text against the old, so a byte-exact revert is accepted; and the `cite: Option<Vec<String>>` parameter exists precisely so an author can add a citation to existing prose, its doc comment saying that without it "`tetel review`'s own instruction (`mint the missing claim and cite it`) [was] unreachable for existing prose" — so a citation-only revision is unrefused and encouraged, as the claim says. The in-proof predicate the claim names is the one `analyze_ledger` uses, digest-based with the empty digest grandfathered. The qualification is recorded separately against F4: the stated execution result on tet29's logs does not reproduce.

The rule, the two-part text-timestamp definition, the existential clause (b), "both shipped memos list nothing as they stand", and all four constructed listings against tet29's P11 (rewrite; citation-only revision adding an in-proof claim; adding a record-less claim; the uncited-paragraph dual) reproduce exactly. The clause that fails is "the one real post-pass prose revision in either of them, tet29's P4 at 1786174635". tet28's P18 has the identical shape: text timestamp 1786132480, later than cited C6's first proof at 1786132166, saved from listing only because clause (c) takes the maximum over C13's first proof at 1786133118 — and its `why` records the same fix-round cause ("C13 was narrowed after grounding pass k1 qualified..."). There are two such revisions across the two memos, not one; the substantive point (each is correctly not listed, for the max-taking reason) holds for both.
Clause (b)'s in-proof predicate is exactly analyze_ledger's grading_current test: digest == sha256(current proposition), empty digest grandfathered.

The rule, the predicate it borrows from `analyze_ledger`, the append-only/citation-only-revision reasoning, "both shipped memos list nothing as they stand", the two named revisions and their stated non-listing reasons, and all four constructed tet29 P11 cases reproduce exactly when I implement the rule independently. One clause is wrong: "the two real post-pass prose revisions they contain between them" undercounts. tet28's P2 is a third — a paragraph revised at 1786132471, after tet28's first evidence record at 1786132471's predecessor 1786131782, with `why` "C1 was narrowed after grounding pass k1 qualified…", i.e. a fix-round rewrite of exactly the kind P18 and P4 are. It is correctly unlisted for the very reason C4 gives (C1's first in-proof record is at 1786132541, later than the rewrite), so the conclusion is unharmed — but the enumeration and the count "two" are not accurate. Separately, whether the author's own testing used constructions appended to tet29's logs is a fact about their workspace I cannot witness; I could only confirm its premise, that neither shipped memo contains a real fix-round rewrite the rule catches.

prop: The residue is about any prose whose text postdates the settling of what it cites, not about revision specifically: the block's timestamp is the one that set its current text, whether that was its `Create` or its last `Revise`, both of which carry a `timestamp` on the prose event. Including creations closes an identical exposure at near-zero cost in listings. It is identical because a paragraph written fresh under already-graded claims rests on them exactly as ungradedly as a rewritten one. It is near-zero cost because a paragraph created in a fix round to carry a new assertion normally cites a new claim, and a new claim is not in proof when the paragraph is written; by the time any pass has put it in proof, that first proof postdates the paragraph, so the block never becomes listable. What creation-counting does catch is the case worth catching: a new paragraph written under nothing but old, already-settled claims.
note: The evidence shows that both `Create` and `Revise` prose events carry timestamps, but `load_all` discards those timestamps from `Block`, and it does not establish the asserted listing behavior, near-zero cost, or universal timing of newly created claims becoming proven. Thus the event-level premise is supported while the broader residue and cost claims are not settled.

later.note: The mechanical half is witnessed: both `ProseEvent::Create` and `ProseEvent::Revise` carry `timestamp: u64` (F3, prose.rs:41-73), so "the block's timestamp is the one that set its current text, whether that was its Create or its last Revise" is implementable exactly as stated, and the rule I executed does take max(Create, latest Revise) (F6). What I cannot establish from source is the cost/benefit reasoning that the rest of the proposition asserts — that including creations is "near-zero cost in listings" because a fix-round paragraph normally cites a new claim not yet in proof. That is a claim about authoring behaviour, and the two shipped memos give no instance of it: their residue is empty under a rule that already counts creations (F6), which is consistent with the assertion but does not exhibit a single created-in-a-fix-round paragraph either being caught or being spared. The word "normally" is not measured anywhere I could reach.

Case A shows a never-revised Create is listed on its creation timestamp; cases B and C show a paragraph written before the pass that first proves its new claim is unlistable even when it also cites an already-settled claim, which is exactly the no-inflation argument. The proposition's own final sentences concede that authoring frequency is unmeasured.
ProseEvent::Create and ProseEvent::Revise both carry `timestamp: u64`, which is what makes the derivation indifferent to which kind of event bears the current text.
Both ProseEvent::Create and ProseEvent::Revise declare timestamp: u64, so the derivation is indifferent to which variant bore the current text.

A pure Create after settling is listed; a block whose cited claim is not yet in proof contributes no anchor and cannot be listed, and once that claim enters proof its first proof postdates the creation, so the block stays unlisted either way.

Both event variants carry a `timestamp` (F2), so the derivation is indifferent to Create-vs-Revise; and running the rule over tet29's real logs with synthetic creations confirms all three consequences C5 draws — a fresh paragraph under only settled claims is listed, one written before the pass that proved its new claim is not, and it is still not listed when it also cites a settled claim, because the anchor is a maximum. C5's own disclaimer about how often fix-round paragraphs take that shape is stated as unmeasured, which is accurate.

src/prose.rs is byte-identical at the pin and in the worktree. `ProseEvent` has exactly the two variants the proposition names, and both carry `timestamp: u64` — Create at line 61, Revise at line 73 — so a per-block "earliest event bearing the current text" is derivable from the log with no regard to which variant it is, exactly as stated.

prop: The first-proof anchor makes the line unclearable by anything that did not look at the prose, and that is deliberate: a further grounding pass over unchanged wording appends records with later timestamps but cannot move the earliest one, so re-grounding never blesses a listed block. The only two things that clear it are reverting the text, and revising or adding a cited claim and having the new wording graded — which is exactly the remedy the finding calls for, since the defect is prose asserting something no claim carries. The cost, stated rather than hidden: a listing has no cheap discharge, so a flow-only edit made after a memo's claims have settled stays listed until the memo's next claim revision, and a memo shipped with such an edit ships the line. This is a smaller version of a cost this project has already paid badly once — `no scope declared` printed one undischargeable line per claim and buried the findings that were about the document under a constant — but it differs where it matters: this line is about *this* document, never fires on all blocks at once, and names two concrete acts that clear it.
note: The evidence supports the first-proof/minimum-timestamp behavior and the cost of a later flow-only edit, but “the only two things” is too absolute: blocks with no citations or with headings are skipped by the reporting logic, and matching can depend on the citation tuple as well as the text.

later.note: The unclearable-by-re-grounding half is right: evidence is strictly appended with a fresh now_unix per record, so a later pass cannot move a claim's earliest in-proof timestamp (F7). The precedent half is right too: the `no scope declared` line did fire once per claim on every tetel-authored memo — "eight identical lines on the first real memo" — and was collapsed to one document-level line for the stated reason (F8). But the clause "The only two things that clear it are reverting the text, and revising or adding a cited claim" is false under this design's own rule. Prose history is append-only and clause (d) reads the timestamp of the event that set the block's current text; a revert is a new `Revise` with a new, later timestamp, so on tet29's real logs a block edited to 1786176064 and then reverted byte-for-byte at 1786176364 is still listed against the same anchor 1786174494 (F8). Reverting clears the line only under a different clause (d) — earliest event whose text equals the current text — which is not what C4/C5 state; C5 explicitly says the timestamp is the Create or the *last* Revise. So the enumeration of remedies has one member, not two, and the stated cost is correspondingly worse than the proposition admits.

"Under the repaired definition of a block's text timestamp ... exactly two things clear a listing" is false, and the repair is what makes the third one work. A citation-only prose revision — byte-identical text, a replacement cite list — leaves the block's text timestamp exactly where it was, because the repaired definition takes the earliest event whose text equals the current text, and changes the right-hand side of clause (d) instead. Executed against tet29's real logs: P11 rewritten at 1786174700 with no claim touched is LISTED (anchor 1786174494, cites C13); appending `C4` to its cite list — a claim already in proof since 1786175367 because a later pass genuinely regraded it — clears the listing outright. No text changed, nothing new was graded, nothing was revised for the purpose, and no machine check fires. In a fix round there is always such a claim: the one the round revised. The paragraph the residue exists to surface is laundered by pointing it at someone else's honest work. A fourth clearer follows from clause (c) rather than (d): appending a brand-new claim with no evidence at all also clears the listing, and per F2 a record-less claim is `ungrounded` — human-owed, never a machine failure — so that escape is red-free too. Note the pre-repair definition did not have this hole: a citation-only revision would have pushed the timestamp to now and the block would have stayed listed. The repair to C6 opened a second defect in C6.

The mechanism behind the refutation above, witnessed in source. `prose::revise` refuses exactly two things — an unknown block id and an empty `--why`. It does not compare the new text against the block's current text, so a revision supplying byte-identical text is accepted and appended; and `ProseEvent::Revise` carries `cite: Option<Vec<String>>`, which `load_all` applies as `b.cite = c`, a wholesale replacement. So a block's citation set is read off the LAST event that set it while its text timestamp is read off the EARLIEST event bearing the current text. C6 treats the citation set as fixed and reasons only about what can move the timestamp; it is the other side of clause (d) that is freely mutable at zero cost. This is also the documented remedial path: prose.rs's own doc on the `cite` parameter says it exists so that `tetel review`'s instruction "mint the missing claim and cite it" is reachable for existing prose.

Everything about unclearability holds as executed: re-grounding on unchanged wording leaves P11 listed (the anchor is a minimum, and a later duplicate record cannot move it), a citation-only revision to an in-proof claim lists rather than clears, a record-less citation contributes no anchor, and only a byte-exact revert or moving the evidence clears. The clause that fails as written is "never fires on all blocks at once". tet29's shipped prose is 12 blocks, all non-heading and all cited; appending one post-proof flow-edit revision to each lists all 12 of 12. The rule does not structurally exclude a whole-document listing — what distinguishes it from `no scope declared` is that it is conditional on what the author did, not that a full sweep is impossible.

The clearing/non-clearing behaviours C6 enumerates all reproduce: citation-only revision to an in-proof claim lists, record-less citation adds no anchor, byte-exact revert clears because the timestamp is looked up by content over an append-only log.

The `no scope declared` history C6 cites is in report.rs: the collapsed one-per-document bullet carries the comment "repeating it per row buried the findings that are about *this* document under a constant".

Constructions 2-5 are exactly the four dispositions this claim asserts: a further pass over unchanged wording keeps the listing, a citation-only revision adding an in-proof claim lists rather than clears, a record-less citation does not silence, and a byte-exact revert clears.
Flow-editing every one of tet29's twelve blocks lists all twelve, so nothing in the rule bounds the count.
The `no scope declared` line was indeed collapsed from once-per-claim to one document-level line, which is the comparison this claim distinguishes itself from.

Every positive behaviour C6 asserts reproduces: re-grounding unchanged wording does not clear a listing, a citation-only revision lists rather than clears, a record-less citation does not suppress, byte-exact revert clears, a revised-and-regraded claim clears, and flow-editing all of tet29 lists 12 of 12. The `no scope declared` collapse precedent it appeals to is in report.rs with the quoted reason. The clause I cannot support as written is the exhaustiveness: "Two things clear a listing", and the opening "unclearable by anything that did not either restore the settled text or move the evidence". A third act clears one — withdrawing every claim a listed block cites. Withdrawn claims are filtered out of the rendered ledger, so clause (b) finds nothing in proof and the block is skipped; simulated, dropping P11's sole cited claim takes the residue from ['P11'] to []. That neither restores the text nor moves any evidence. It does leave a "cited but undefined" line, but report.rs prints that in the human-owed partition, so nothing fails.

prop: This is the first check to compare timestamps across processes, and the comparison is sound in unit but not in clock. Both sides are produced by a `now_unix` that is byte-identical in the two places it is defined — `SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).map(|d| d.as_secs()).unwrap_or(0)` at evidence.rs:288 and workspace.rs:257, the only two definitions in the worktree — so they are the same unit and epoch, UTC seconds, with no timezone term. What no record establishes is that the two processes kept the same wall clock; `SystemTime::now()` reads the clock of whoever called it. The bound is therefore exact and must be printed rather than implied: an ordering this line reports can be wrong only if the grounding process's clock differed from the authoring workspace's by more than the interval between the prose edit and the pass that first put the cited claims in proof. That interval is the anchor's own doing — first proof rather than last pass puts a whole grounding round between the two events in the case the residue exists for — but nothing in the data bounds it from below, so no claim is made that it is large.
note: The two `now_unix` implementations are semantically identical and use Unix-epoch seconds, but they are not byte-identical: `evidence.rs` formats the method chain across multiple lines while `workspace.rs` keeps it on one line.

later.note: The substance holds: there are exactly two `fn now_unix` definitions in the worktree, at evidence.rs:288 and workspace.rs:257, both `SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).map(|d| d.as_secs()).unwrap_or(0)`, so the two sides are the same unit and epoch (UTC seconds, no timezone term), and nothing establishes the two processes shared a wall clock — `SystemTime::now()` reads the caller's clock. Two clauses are wrong as written. (a) "byte-identical in the two places it is defined": the bytes differ — workspace.rs:257 is `pub fn` with the chain on one line, evidence.rs:288 is a private `fn` with the same chain split across four indented lines. The expressions are token-identical, not byte-identical. (b) "This is the first check to compare timestamps across processes": `facts::mint_windows` already compares a `FactEvent::Create` timestamp from facts.jsonl against refusals.log timestamps (`ts <= *minted_at`), and each mint and each refusal is a separate process invocation. What is genuinely new is comparing an *authoring-side* clock against a *grounding-side* clock, which is not what the sentence says.

Both stated line numbers are exact (workspace.rs:257 pub fn, one-line body; evidence.rs:288 private fn, four-line body), the chains are token-for-token identical, mint_windows is the named precedent and is workspace-local, and EvidenceRecord::timestamp is explicitly read by no check. `SystemTime::now()` reading the caller's clock and the unbounded-from-below interval are both stated as limits rather than claims, which is what the code supports.

analyze_ledger is the check that compares a claim against its evidence, and it does so by sha256 digest, never by timestamp — C7's "every check that could have compared a claim against its evidence has used a digest instead".

workspace.rs:257 is the one-line `pub fn now_unix`; evidence.rs:288 is the private four-line one; the SystemTime chain is token-for-token identical, so same unit and epoch, UTC seconds, no timezone term, and each reads its own caller's clock.
facts::mint_windows does compare a mint timestamp against refusals.log timestamps written by separate invocations, and both logs belong to one workspace.

A whole-source search for `timestamp` finds no other comparison site: no existing check orders an authoring timestamp against a grounding-pass one, and the evidence record's timestamp is read by nothing.

`mint_windows` does order timestamps written by separate invocations (fact mints against refusals.log lines) and does it inside one workspace; and a survey of checks.rs, scope.rs, worldstate.rs, evidence.rs, review.rs and citations.rs finds no timestamp comparison at all, with the identity `born` field never read by a check — so no existing check compares an authoring clock against a grounding pass's, and claim-versus-evidence is done by digest in `analyze_ledger`.

The line references are exact: workspace.rs:257 is the `pub fn` with its body on one line, evidence.rs:288 is a private fn whose identical chain runs over four lines, and the expression is token-for-token the same — UTC seconds since the Unix epoch with no timezone term. The prose side is stamped by the first and the evidence side by the second, and both call `SystemTime::now()`, which reads the calling process's own clock and records nothing about which clock that was. So "sound in unit but not in clock" is exactly right, and the stated bound follows.

prop: There is no digest-shaped alternative in the sharp sense, and the reason is structural rather than an omission: `out_of_proof` can compare digests because a record carries a digest of the very text it graded, whereas nothing in the record shape names or digests a prose block — not `Subject`, not `Predicate`, not `RecordInput` — and the grounding brief deliberately hands a pass only id, proposition and pin. Giving a record a prose digest would require the grounding pass to read the prose it is supposed to grade blind. A weaker, genuinely clock-free alternative is constructible: have `render --out` append a publication record — per prose block its text digest, per claim its proposition digest and whether anything grades it — so the residue becomes an ordinal comparison between successive publications with no clock anywhere. It is rejected on resolution, not on cost. A publication log samples state only at the renders the author happens to perform, so a prose edit and the grading that preceded it inside one publication interval are indistinguishable, and the FORK-94 shape — grounding pass, then fix-round prose, then one render — falls entirely inside a single interval and would be missed. The timestamp comparison resolves exactly that ordering, which is why it is worth its stated bound.
note: No evidence was captured, so the structural claims, the proposed publication-log alternative, and the timestamp-resolution comparison cannot be established or contradicted.

later.note: Second record for the brief clause: brief::build returns only id, proposition and pin per claim, so a pass is handed no prose at all.

Subject, Predicate and RecordInput each read in full: no field names or digests a prose block, exactly as the proposition states, and the proposition itself disclaims completeness ("not a claim that no third exists").

BriefItem carries exactly id, proposition and pin, and the module doc says scope is withheld "so an independent grounding pass can't see what the author declared the claim ranges over" — the brief hands a pass only id, proposition and pin, so a prose digest would require the pass to read the prose it grades blind.

The structural half is exactly as stated and I confirmed it field by field: `Subject` carries only `name` (the claim id) and `digest` (sha256 of the claim proposition); `Predicate` carries verdict, pass, reported_kind, source, extent, world, note, pin, timestamp; `RecordInput` carries claim, pass, verdict, reported_kind, source, extent, note, pin. Nothing on any of the three names or digests a prose block, and `brief::build` hands a pass only `BriefItem { id, proposition, pin }`. What I could not establish is the rejection of the second alternative. That the publication-log design would miss the case rests on "the FORK-94 shape — grounding pass, then fix-round prose, then one render", which is an external trail this pass has no access to; and no publication-record mechanism exists in this tree to examine, so the resolution argument against it is reasoning rather than something source can settle. The claim's own hedge ("this is not a claim that no third exists") is honest and I am not disputing it.
Subject carries only name + sha256 of the proposition; Predicate and RecordInput carry no prose field of any kind. Nothing in the record shape names or digests a prose block.

BriefItem carries exactly id, proposition and pin, so "the grounding brief deliberately hands a pass only id, proposition and pin" is exact, and with F7 the sharp alternative's structural impossibility is established. The clause I cannot establish is "Per the ticket's own account of the FORK-94 trail ... that is the shape the finding took": the ticket is in a planning repository this pass must not open. The resolution argument against the publication-record alternative is reasoning about a mechanism that does not exist in this tree, so there is nothing here to read it against either — but it is stated as reasoning, not as an observation.

The structural obstruction is exactly as stated: `Subject` carries one name and one digest slot filled from the proposition, `Predicate` and `RecordInput` carry no prose field at all, and `BriefItem` hands a pass only id, proposition and pin — so a prose-digest record would require the grounder to digest prose it was never shown. The rejection of the publication-record alternative is an analytic property of any interval-sampled log (state only at render moments, so two events inside one interval are unorderable), which the proposition states correctly and does not overclaim; it also explicitly disclaims that no third alternative exists, and flags the FORK-94 shape as the ticket's report rather than establishing it.

prop: The vacuous cases are excluded by the in-proof gate rather than by a special case, and the exclusion is justified by non-overlap: a claim with no records at all is already printed as `ungrounded`, and a claim whose every record grades superseded text is already a machine failure as `out_of_proof`, so a prose block resting on either is already in front of the reader under a line that says something truer about it. Requiring every cited claim to be in proof therefore makes a memo with no evidence ledger, and a memo mid-first-draft, list nothing at all — the residue is empty until a memo has been graded, which is when it starts being able to say anything. Two populations fall outside the rule and are worth naming rather than counting: heading blocks, and paragraphs that cite nothing. A paragraph with no citation is the one place a false assertion can sit with no citation edge to compare against, so its invisibility here is a real gap and belongs in the printed non-coverage list, not in a footnote.
note: The checks explicitly classify claims with no records as `ungrounded` and claims whose records all grade superseded text as `out_of_proof`, while the prose residue requires every cited claim to have proof and skips headings and uncited blocks. The report’s printed `NON_COVERAGE` section accounts for the uncited-paragraph gap.

later.note: Second record for the non-overlap clause: `ungrounded_claims` prints "ungrounded — no evidence record on file" in the human-owed partition and `out_of_proof` is one of the eleven fields in `machine_check_failed`, so a claim with no records and a claim whose every record is stale are each already in front of the reader under their own line.

The non-overlap justification holds only for a block ALL of whose citations are ungrounded or out of proof, but the gate C9 defends is universally quantified ("Requiring every cited claim to be in proof"). For a block citing nine settled claims and one record-less one, the substitute line the reader gets is `ungrounded: C99` — a statement about a claim, not about the paragraph, and in no sense "truer about it" than the residue line it displaced, which would have said this paragraph's text postdates every settled claim it rests on. Escape B above shows this is not merely a gap but an actuator: appending one record-less claim to a listed block's cite list removes it from the residue while adding only a human-owed `ungrounded` line and no machine failure. The exclusion needs the condition stated, or the gate needs to be per-citation rather than all-or-nothing.
Both vacuous cases list nothing with no special rule — the in-proof test alone produces the behaviour.
Heading blocks (case D) and paragraphs citing nothing (case E) fall outside the rule entirely, the two populations C9 names as non-covered.

Measured on BSD grep 2.6.0-FreeBSD: a file named explicitly on the command line is skipped when `--exclude` matches it (no output, exit 1, against output and exit 0 for the identical command without the flag), and a directory named explicitly as the recursion root is skipped when `--exclude-dir` matches it (same contrast). Only one of the three cases behaves the way the constraint describes: `--exclude-dir` does not suppress a file inside an excluded directory when that file is named explicitly and searched non-recursively.
note: The command contrasts directly show that matching `--exclude` skips an explicitly named file, matching `--exclude-dir` skips an explicitly named directory root, while an explicitly named file inside an excluded directory is still read. However, the captured evidence does not identify the `/usr/bin/grep` version as BSD grep 2.6.0-FreeBSD.

prop: The rendered-memo exclusion the ticket sketches — "one glob for `*.tetel` directories under the search root, with the suffix stripped, passed as `--exclude`" — is unsound as written, in two independent ways measured on BSD grep 2.6.0-FreeBSD. First, a pattern must be spelled the way grep constructs the file's name from the root as given: with a relative root, an absolute-path `--exclude` excluded nothing at all and the search returned every file, while the same path spelled relative to the root excluded exactly the intended file. Second, a suffix-stripped bare basename over-excludes: `--exclude='memo.md'` removed both a genuine rendered memo and an unrelated other/memo.md that has no sibling other/memo.md.tetel and so is not a rendered memo under the ticket's own test. The exclusion must therefore be emitted path-prefixed in the root's own spelling, never as a basename.
note: The outputs show that an absolute exclusion matched nothing under relative root '.', while './docs/design/memo.md' excluded the intended file. They also show bare 'memo.md' excluded both docs/design/memo.md and unrelated other/memo.md, despite the latter lacking a .tetel sibling.

prop: The exclusion disclosure can be made durable with no schema change, by writing it into the whole-search record's `label`. Two existing mechanisms carry it from there: `compose::render_facts` builds the committed memo's "Extent (captured)" column by joining extent entries' `label` fields and renders nothing else from an entry — not the `key`, not the captured output — so a label reaches every reader of the committed document; and `facts::mint` hashes each pending entry's `label` (followed by `world_root`, `world_state` and `output`) into the pin, so two searches whose exclusion sets differ pin differently even when their matched output is byte-identical.
note: The evidence supports that `render_facts` emits only extent labels and that `facts::mint` hashes each label before the world markers and output. It does not establish that the whole-search label actually encodes the exclusion set, or that differing exclusion sets therefore always produce distinct pins.

prop: The rendered-memo enumeration is affordable, because it is a directory-only walk while the grep it precedes must open and read every file. On the tetel worktree — 848 directories, 159,519 files, three `*.tetel` snapshot directories — enumerating the snapshot directories took 0.130s against 3.953s for a single census grep with `look_grep`'s own flags over the same root. On the one failure mode measured, an unreadable directory, the walk and the grep are bounded identically: a chmod-000 directory hiding an `x.tetel` subdirectory produced "Permission denied" from both. Whether the two walks agree on any other traversal difference — symlinked directories in particular — was not measured here.
note: No evidence was provided or captured, so the performance figures, directory/file counts, permission-error comparison, and traversal caveat cannot be verified.

later.note: Counts reconstruct exactly (the tree now shows 849/159,528/four only because this memo's own snapshot, ledger and file were added since; the delta is exactly 9 files and 1 directory). The affordability relation reproduces a fortiori — 0.149s enumeration against 15.297s census here — though the two absolute timings differ from the design's 0.130s/3.953s single run, which a later run cannot contradict. The permission-denied parity and the final "not measured" disclaimer about symlinked directories both hold as written.

The affordability finding reproduces; three stated counts do not, and one stated identity is looser than measured. Today the same tree is 853 directories, 159,534 files and FOUR `*.tetel` snapshot directories, not "848 directories, 159,519 files, three" — the fourth snapshot is tet46's own, untracked. Timing reproduces closely: 0.13s for the directory-only walk against 3.64s for one census grep with look_grep's flags (design: 0.130s / 3.953s). On the chmod-000 case, both the walk and the grep do print "Permission denied" for the same directory, but they are not "bounded identically" in the strict sense: find exits 1 and grep exits 2. The unmeasured-symlink caveat the claim itself states is correct — I did not test that either.

prop: The ticket's central measurement reproduces on this tree, and the three exclusions together remove tetel's own output from a census without removing source. A census of the symbol NON_COVERAGE over the tetel worktree with `look_grep`'s flags returned 87 lines / 858,096 bytes from 15 files, of which 14 were tetel's own output — three rendered memos, three evidence ledgers, eight snapshot .jsonl files — and exactly one, src/report.rs, was source. With `--exclude-dir='*.tetel'`, `--exclude='*.evidence.jsonl'` and one path-spelled `--exclude` per stripped snapshot directory, the same census returned 2 lines / 169 bytes, from src/report.rs alone.
note: The captured census lists exactly 87 lines and 858,096 bytes across 15 matching files, with 14 under the three memo/output structures and only src/report.rs outside them. Applying the stated exclusions leaves exactly 2 lines and 169 bytes, both from src/report.rs, so the source match is retained.

later.note: Everything except the pre-exclusion size reproduces exactly. Re-running the same NON_COVERAGE census with look_grep's flags today returns 115 lines / 2,565,015 bytes from 21 files, not "87 lines / 858,096 bytes from 15 files"; the six extra files are precisely the tet46 memo's own artifacts (.md, .evidence.jsonl, four .tetel/*.jsonl), which are untracked and did not exist when the design measured. Set those aside and the file set is exactly the 15 claimed, with exactly the claimed composition — three rendered memos, three evidence ledgers, eight snapshot .jsonl, and src/report.rs as the sole source. The post-exclusion figure is exact: 2 lines / 169 bytes, src/report.rs alone. So the clause I cannot establish is the specific "87 lines / 858,096 bytes"; the substance and every other figure hold.

prop: A change confined to `look_grep` cannot alter how an already-committed memo checks, for two independent reasons. The first is call-graph isolation: two exhaustive greps of the whole `src/` tree show `Command::new` matching in only `observe.rs` (the grep inside `look_grep`, and `run_command`'s child) and `worldstate.rs` (git), and `observe::` matching in only `main.rs` and `mcp.rs`, which build a `LookRequest` and dispatch it, and `facts.rs`, where the sole occurrence is inside a doc comment — so every other file in `src/`, including every file on the check and render paths, neither calls into `observe` by that path nor spawns a process by that constructor. The second is immutability: the `tetel fact` module doc states that a revision rewrites the note only, and that "extent, output and pin are set once at mint time and never appear in a revision event at all, so there is no code path that could change them later either". A fact minted under the old behaviour therefore keeps the extent and pin it was minted with, whatever a later `look` would now do.
note: The greps enumerate exactly the stated `Command::new` and `observe::` occurrences, including the doc-comment-only occurrence in `facts.rs` and the dispatch sites in `main.rs` and `mcp.rs`. The `facts.rs` module documentation explicitly states that revisions rewrite only the note and never alter extent, output, or pin, so facts minted under prior behavior retain those values.

prop: TET-28's census requirement is currently priced by tetel's own output rather than by the symbol being censused. Measured over the tetel worktree with `look_grep`'s own flags, whole-worktree censuses of `look_grep`, `NON_COVERAGE`, `censuses`, `look_path` and `search_key` return 709,469 / 858,096 / 691,562 / 688,776 / 633,291 bytes respectively — a shared floor of roughly 0.63 MB that is present whichever symbol is sought — and dropping snapshot directories and evidence ledgers alone reduces each to between 931 and 34,595 bytes, removing 95.9% to 99.9% of what the search returned. Those are bytes the search returns from grep and bytes the fact then stores; how many of them reach any particular caller's context is a separate quantity this claim does not assert.
note: No evidence was provided, so the claim's pricing behavior and reported byte counts cannot be verified or settled.

later.note: The structure holds and the numbers do not. Re-measuring all five symbols today with look_grep's own flags gives 2,498,237 / 2,565,015 / 2,388,485 / 2,377,267 / 2,322,381 bytes, not "709,469 / 858,096 / 691,562 / 688,776 / 633,291", and the shared floor is roughly 2.32 MB rather than "roughly 0.63 MB"; dropping snapshot directories and evidence ledgers alone leaves 4,267-47,465 bytes rather than "between 931 and 34,595". What does reproduce, unchanged: a floor of tetel's own output is present whichever symbol is sought, and the two exclusions remove 98.15%-99.82% of each search — inside the stated 95.9%-99.9% band. The divergence is fully accounted for by tet46's own memo, evidence ledger and snapshot now existing in docs/design (six additional matched files), i.e. by exactly the churn the claim is about; but the specific byte figures as written are not what the same commands return at this HEAD.

prop: Capping what a fact stores and capping what a `look` returns are already separable in practice, and only the return path currently has any cap at all — imposed downstream, not by tetel. Taking this design's one census, `look --grep look_grep` rooted at the tetel worktree, the search succeeded and was recorded, but the agent harness refused to return the result, reporting 707,751 characters across 38 lines as exceeding its maximum allowed tokens and spilling it to a file; the author therefore never read the output of their own census, while the full captured output was nonetheless minted into the fact and ships in the snapshot. The census's own extent shows why: of the ten files matched, eight are tetel's own output — three snapshot `facts.jsonl`, one snapshot `claims.jsonl`, one snapshot `prose.jsonl`, two evidence ledgers and one rendered memo — and two, `src/observe.rs` and `src/worldstate.rs`, are source.
note: The evidence supports that the census matched ten files, that tetel captured the output, and that the return was rejected downstream at 707,751 characters. It does not establish the stronger assertion that the author therefore never read the spilled output, nor does it prove that no other cap exists anywhere.

later.note: Reproduced independently: the same census on the same client was refused by the harness with a character count and a spill file, while the search was recorded in full; the design's 707,751 characters / 38 lines / 10 files, and the exact composition (eight tetel artifacts, src/observe.rs and src/worldstate.rs), reconstruct byte-exactly once this memo's own artifacts are filtered out. The only clause I could not witness is that the *author* never read their own output, which is a fact about their session.

Source side of the separability claim: look_grep's return is `printed.push_str(&stdout)` with no cap, and the per-file pending entries carry `output: matches.join("\n")` with no cap either — so tetel imposes no bound on either path, and any bound that fires is the caller's.

The extent breakdown is exact and the size/harness clauses are not checkable here. Re-running the census `look_grep`-pattern search over the tetel worktree today and setting aside the six tet46 artifacts that did not exist at measurement time yields precisely the ten files claimed, in precisely the claimed composition: three snapshot facts.jsonl, one snapshot claims.jsonl, one snapshot prose.jsonl, two evidence ledgers, one rendered memo, and src/observe.rs plus src/worldstate.rs as the two source files. What I cannot establish is the clause "reporting 707,751 characters across 38 lines as exceeding its maximum allowed tokens and spilling it to a file" — that is an event in the author's own client session, not something recoverable from this repository, and the same search now returns 110 lines / 2,498,237 bytes. I deliberately did not reproduce it by taking a multi-hundred-kilobyte `look` myself, since minting that would put the whole output permanently into a snapshot.
The source half: look_grep copies the whole grep stdout into LookOutcome with no cap of any kind, so no cap on what a fact stores or on what a look returns exists inside tetel.

prop: The explicit-path exception must be implemented as a decision about whether to pass exclusion flags at all, and `look_grep`'s existing shape already supplies the discriminator. `look_grep` adds `-r` only when `root_path.is_dir()`, and passes `root` through to grep verbatim as the caller spelled it, never canonicalized. So the rule is: when the root is not a directory the caller has named a single file explicitly, and no exclusion flag is passed — which is required, since `--exclude` otherwise suppresses a file named on the command line. When the root is a directory that is itself tetel content, again no exclusion flag is passed — which is required, since `--exclude-dir` otherwise suppresses a directory named as the recursion root. A root counts as tetel content by three format tests and no others: some component of it ends with the literal `.tetel`, or its filename ends with `.evidence.jsonl`, or a directory named by appending `.tetel` to it exists. Only in the remaining case, a directory root that is not itself tetel content, are the three exclusions passed, and each must be spelled the way grep will construct the matched file's name from that same root string.
note: No evidence was captured, so the claim cannot be verified or refuted.

later.note: The discriminator exists exactly as described: `if root_path.is_dir() { args.push("-r") }` is the only place recursion is decided, and `args.push(root)` passes the caller's own spelling through with no canonicalization, so a design that keys on is_dir and spells exclusions against `root` has both inputs already in hand.

Both "which is required" sub-clauses are measured, not asserted: --exclude does suppress a file named on the command line (exit 1 vs exit 0), and --exclude-dir does suppress a directory named as the recursion root (exit 1 vs exit 0), so withholding the flags in those two cases is forced rather than merely chosen.

prop: The ticket's headline reframing — that census output cost "~135k tokens, roughly 40% of the designer's reported 336k run" — is not reproducible from this design's evidence, and this run produced a direct counter-instance rather than merely failing to confirm it. `look_grep`'s return is genuinely uncapped in tetel: `printed.push_str(&stdout)` copies the grep's whole stdout into what `LookOutcome` hands back, with no length check, truncation or configuration between them. But when this design took a real whole-worktree census, the client harness rejected the 707,751-character result and returned roughly 1,300 characters of error text naming a spill file instead. So a large census's bytes need not enter a model's context at all, and the uncapped return does not by itself establish any figure in tokens. Two things remain true and are worth more than the figure: the bound that fired belongs to the caller rather than to tetel, and a different caller will not supply one; and nothing in `look_grep` records that anything downstream bounded what it returned, so a truncation leaves no trace in the fact it was minted into.
note: No opened evidence or captured output is provided, so the claimed counter-instance and the assertions about `look_grep`, the caller bound, and the spill-file rejection cannot be verified from this record.

later.note: `printed.push_str(&stdout)` in look_grep copies grep's whole stdout with no length check, truncation or configuration, and nothing in the function records that a downstream consumer bounded what it returned — the pending entries are written and LookOutcome returned identically either way.

The counter-instance reproduces: the whole-worktree census was rejected by the client and replaced with a short error naming a spill file, so the census's bytes did not enter the model's context and the uncapped return establishes no token figure. The "~135k tokens / 40% of 336k" figure is nowhere derivable from what I could observe either, which is what the claim asserts.

The source clauses hold exactly: `printed.push_str(&stdout)` copies grep's whole stdout into what LookOutcome returns with no length check, truncation or configuration between them, and nothing in look_grep records that anything downstream bounded the return — so a truncation would leave no trace in the minted fact. The clause I cannot establish is the counter-instance itself: "the client harness rejected the 707,751-character result and returned roughly 1,300 characters of error text naming a spill file instead" happened in the author's own client session and is not recoverable from this repository; I did not reproduce it, because taking and minting a ~700 KB look would write that output permanently into a snapshot. Without it, this pass confirms only that the ~135k-token figure is not derivable from tetel's source, not that a direct counter-instance was observed.

prop: `check`'s standing non-coverage list needs a second line rather than an amendment to the one it has. The existing entry reads "whatever the platform's grep skipped — symlinked directories and binary files bound what a whole-worktree search physically visited": both causes it names are platform accidents, and nothing in it contemplates something tetel itself declined to visit. The list's own census block explains its purpose as saying what a census "cannot see", "because a refusal that fired is easily read as coverage it never claimed" — which is exactly the reason a deliberate exclusion must appear, and exactly the reason it must not be folded into the accident line. Every entry is a static string and none is per-search, so the standing line can only say that the policy exists; what a given search actually excluded is not something this list can carry.
note: The evidence supports that the existing entry covers system-grep/platform traversal limits, that the census block is meant to state its blind spots, and that NON_COVERAGE is a static standing list. It does not establish the stronger assertion that tetel has a distinct deliberate exclusion requiring a second line, and the list already separately mentions undeclared modification targets.

prop: TET-28's census predicate needs no change, and this is what makes the two disclosures divide cleanly. `ExtentEntry::censuses` reads exactly five things — that the kind is `Search` or `NoMatch`, that the pattern byte-equals the symbol, that `world_root` is non-empty and not `NO_GIT`, and that `key == world_root` — and never reads `label` or `output`. A worktree-rooted search therefore still censuses after this change, correctly, because the predicate was always about a search's existence and rooting rather than about what it found. What changes is not the predicate but what a passing census entitles a reader to conclude, and that is carried by text: a standing line in `check` saying the exclusion policy exists, and the search record's own `label` saying which patterns this particular search was given.
note: F11 shows that `censuses` checks exactly the kind, pattern, two `world_root` conditions, and key equality, without reading `label` or `output`, and explicitly describes the predicate as about existence and rooting rather than matches. F10 and F13 support the separate disclosure through the rooted search record’s label and the checked non-coverage/exclusion lines.

prop: "No `look` returns tetel's own content" is not the honest name for what this design builds, and the honest name is better rather than merely narrower: a `look` returns tetel's own output only when the caller named it. `look_path` refuses a directory and reads exactly the one file it was given, with no traversal of any kind, so every file it can ever return is one the caller named explicitly and it is left unchanged by this design. `look_grep` is where the whole mechanism lands, and its rule is the same sentence applied to a search — the exclusions are passed only when the root is a directory that is not itself tetel content, so what they remove is only ever reached by traversal. Stating the guarantee over naming rather than over `look`'s two modes covers both with one sentence and does not promise a reader something `look_path` never did.
note: The code shows `look_path` rejects directories and reads only the supplied file, while `look_grep` adds exclusions only for non-TETEL directory roots. The probes confirm excluded TETEL content is skipped during recursive traversal but remains searchable when the file or TETEL directory is explicitly named.

later.note: look_path's half is exact: directory refusal, single fs::read_to_string, no traversal, therefore every file it can return was named by the caller and no exclusion applies to it.

look_grep's half: `-r` is added only when the root is a directory, so traversal — the only way a file the caller did not name can be reached — happens exactly in the case where the design says exclusions are passed.

prop: No opt-out flag should be added, because three escape hatches already exist and each is reached by naming something rather than by setting a flag. `look_path` opens any single named file, including one inside a snapshot, and is untouched by this design. `look --grep` rooted at a path that is itself tetel content passes no exclusions at all, which is not merely permitted but forced: grep's `--exclude-dir` suppresses a directory named as the recursion root, so the flags must be withheld there or naming a snapshot directory would return nothing. And `run` spawns `argv` directly with nothing between the empty-argv refusal and the spawn that inspects, parses or classifies the command or the paths it will touch, so it has no place a path exclusion could be applied even in principle. A flag would add a fourth route that, unlike all three of these, leaves no trace in what was named.
note: The evidence supports the direct `look_path` and `run` behavior and shows that `--exclude-dir` suppresses a snapshot directory used as the recursion root. It does not establish that all exclusions must be withheld (rather than only the root-suppressing one), nor the absolute claim that path exclusion has no possible application in principle.

later.note: Escape hatches 1 and 3: look_path opens any single named file with no traversal and nothing in this design touches it; run_command has only the empty-argv refusal between entry and `Command::new(&argv[0]).spawn()`, with no inspection of the command or its paths, so it offers no place to apply an exclusion.

Escape hatch 2 and its "not merely permitted but forced": measured, `--exclude-dir='*.tetel'` applied to a recursion root that is itself a *.tetel directory returns nothing and exits 1, so the flags must be withheld there or naming a snapshot directory would yield no output.

prop: The pin's non-stationarity is relocated rather than removed, and the relocation is the improvement. Measured on a scratch tree: rendering a second memo into it, changing no source, left the matched output of a search for the same symbol byte-identical while changing the emitted exclusion list from one rendered-memo pattern to two. So the captured output is now stationary against tetel's own churn — which was the ticket's within-run complaint, since an evidence ledger growing during grading no longer reaches the search at all — but the exclusion set is not, and because the design writes that set into the search record's label and the label is inside the pin, two censuses of the same symbol against the same source will still pin differently across a render. The difference is that the cause is now written in plain text in the same record, instead of being an invisible change in what the search happened to read.
note: The scratch run supports byte-identical matches with one versus two emitted exclusions and therefore relocation of the churn. However, the evidence does not establish that tetel’s captured search output itself is stationary or that the exclusion set is written into the search record’s label and thereby changes the pin.

later.note: The "label is inside the pin" step: facts::mint hashes each pending entry's label first in the pin input, so an exclusion set written into the search record's label makes two otherwise identical censuses pin differently.
The pin half: facts::mint hashes each pending entry's label into the pin, so an exclusion set written into the search record's label changes the pin even when the matched output is byte-identical.

prop: A directory containing nothing but tetel's output is still not "explicitly named", and the cost of that is concrete rather than theoretical. `docs/design` holds exactly nine entries — three rendered memos, three evidence ledgers, three snapshot directories — and nothing else. A search rooted there for the symbol `census` returns 184 lines and 1,200,881 bytes today; under this rule it returns nothing and exits 1. The alternative, treating a directory as named when everything beneath it happens to be tetel's, is a judgement about a directory's contents rather than a test on a path, and the project rules that out as a refusal trigger. So the exclusion stays a format test on the root itself, and the price is that searching across memos requires naming a memo file or a snapshot directory rather than the folder they sit in.
note: The evidence supports the nine-entry inventory, the 184-line/1,200,881-byte result, the exclusion result with exit 1, and the fact that exclusions change when another memo is added. It does not establish the asserted project rule that content-based directory treatment is a refusal trigger or directly demonstrate that searches must name a memo file or snapshot directory.

later.note: The "project rules that out" clause is backed by README.md's stated rule that refusals are format-level and never heuristic; a contents-based judgement about a directory is not a decidable format test.

Two clauses do not hold as written today. "docs/design holds exactly nine entries" — it holds twelve, in four triples of the described shape; the extra triple is tet46's own memo/ledger/snapshot, untracked, so the nine was correct before this memo was rendered. And "returns 184 lines and 1,200,881 bytes today" — the same search now returns 260 lines and 2,996,478 bytes. The load-bearing half is exact: with the root docs/design (a directory with no `.tetel` component, so exclusions are passed), the three exclusions leave nothing at all — no output, exit 1, as measured. I did not attempt to verify the separate assertion that "the project rules that out as a refusal trigger", which is a statement about project rules rather than about this repository's source.

prop: The invariance of the three committed memos was demonstrated rather than only argued, against the one input the proposed mechanism actually depends on. `tetel check` was run over tet28's, tet29's and tet30's memos while docs/design held three snapshot directories, and again after this memo was rendered there, making four — a change in exactly the set of tetel artifacts from which the exclusion set would be computed. All three memos produced byte-identical output across the two runs: the same exit code, the same byte count, and the same SHA-256 of combined stdout and stderr (3cdf677b… / 5097feb5… / b3bca4fd…).
note: The evidence demonstrates identical exit codes, byte counts, and hashes for all three memos before and after the directory count changed from three to four. It does not establish that the mechanism actually depends on those snapshot directories, that they determine an exclusion set, or that the added directory resulted from rendering this memo.

later.note: I could not verify the demonstration and could not reproduce its numbers. All three memos do check clean (exit 0) with output that is byte-stable across repeated runs, but at the post-render state the SHA-256 of combined stdout+stderr is 1955453e… / c6cff384… / ade4a129… (14974 / 13095 / 68142 bytes) — none of which begins 3cdf677b, 5097feb5 or b3bca4fd. That mismatch is explainable without contradicting the claim (check's output embeds a "checked by tetel 0.1.0 build …" line, and any difference in binary or capture recipe changes the hash), but it means I am not confirming the quoted values. More fundamentally, the pre-render state — docs/design holding three snapshot directories — no longer exists, so the before/after comparison the claim reports cannot be re-run here at all; the clause "All three memos produced byte-identical output across the two runs" is the one I could not establish.

prop: Every observation in this design was taken against the tetel worktree at commit 043ecb041f02a0d74b90876641eaa573d73a2738 (branch main).
note: The output confirms that the worktree was at commit 043ecb041f02a0d74b90876641eaa573d73a2738 on branch main when the git command ran, but it does not establish that every observation was taken at that commit.

The worktree is verifiably at 043ecb041f02a0d74b90876641eaa573d73a2738 on branch main, with only the untracked tet47 memo artifacts differing — so the tree named is the tree I graded.
