later.note: In `check_file` every named input derives from `path`: the claims from `ledger::import` of the parsed memo, the records from `evidence::load(path)`, the digests from `claim.proposition` inside `analyze_ledger`, and the authoring identity from `workspace::identity_of(&snapshot::snapshot_path(path))`. No other workspace is reached — every further load (`facts`, `targets`, `transplants`, `claims`) is against `snapshot_dir`. `brief_file(path, json)` likewise takes no floor, so any N is the caller's.

check_file derives claims, evidence records, digests and authoring identity from the memo path alone, and every filesystem reach it makes is either the memo or snapshot::snapshot_path(memo); no other workspace is touched. No floor parameter exists in the driver, consistent with N being a caller-supplied policy input.

check_file derives claims, evidence records, digests (via analyze_ledger's sha256 of the claim's own proposition) and authoring identity from the memo path alone, reaching only the snapshot beside the memo; no floor threshold appears in any signature on that path, so N must come from the caller.

check_file derives claims, evidence records, digests (computed in analyze_ledger from claim.proposition) and the authoring identity from the memo path alone, reaching only the memo, its .evidence.jsonl and the snapshot beside it; no floor value appears anywhere in the driver.

prop: Rule 5's matching rule should be the crate's existing `citation_ids_in` rather than a new `C\d+` scan: the existing matcher is already the definition of a row→row citation edge for the dependency-cascade check, it is id-shape-agnostic (a `C\d+` regex would miss real ids of the `R-ROOT` / `CYC-A` shape the crate's own fixtures use, a genuine false-negative class), and its documented error direction is false positives only — which for scheduling means extra grading, never silent under-grading.
note: The evidence supports that the shared matcher is used by `citation_ids_in`, that a `C\d+` scan would miss fixture IDs such as `R-ROOT` and `CYC-A`, and that its documented failure mode is false positives. However, calling it fully id-shape-agnostic overstates the evidence: it still requires an uppercase-leading ID containing a digit or hyphen, and the excerpt does not establish the dependency-cascade definition or scheduling consequence.

later.note: "Its documented error direction is false positives only — which for scheduling means extra grading, never silent under-grading" holds only under a condition the claim does not state: that every inter-claim reference an author writes inside a proposition is bracketed or sits in a whole-line cites trailer. It is not. `scan_line` (src/citations.rs 55-140) enters the id scan only at a `[` byte after the trailer branch declines, so a proposition naming another claim in running prose is silently missed — and this memo's own C13 concedes exactly that. The concession is not a footnote to the error direction, it inverts it: for scheduling, a missed edge is precisely silent under-grading, the failure mode this claim says cannot occur. Measured on the corpus: across 90 claims in the five rendered memos there are zero bracketed citation-shaped ids inside any proposition and four bare prose references, one of them in this memo's own C4 ("the same grandfathering C5 turns on"). So on the observed population the matcher's error direction for rule 5 is false negatives only, not false positives only.

The replacement matcher is specified as "a whitespace- or punctuation-delimited token in a proposition is an edge when it is byte-equal to an id that this document's ledger defines". A hyphen is punctuation, so on any ledger whose ids contain one that tokenisation can never produce a token byte-equal to an id, and the closure yields the empty edge set — the exact defect the claim uses to reject `citation_ids_in`, moved onto a different population. That population is not hypothetical: src/citations.rs 38-55 states the id shape as uppercase-led "with a digit or a hyphen" and names `S3-L17`, `E-4`, `X-6`, `R-ROOT`, `CYC-A` as corpus-ledger ids, two of them "real ids in this crate's own fixtures"; the captured rg sweep returns 21 hyphenated ledger row ids across nine fixture documents and two source modules, with no unhyphenated one among them. Worse for the comparison the claim draws, src/ledger.rs 361-383 — the importer's well-formed-row test — has claim `X-1` with proposition "`foo` returns **4** always [X-2]": a bracketed citation-shaped sibling id inside a proposition, which `citation_ids_in` (src/citations.rs 84-120) does find and the ledger-membership matcher as worded does not. The "not one proposition contains a bracketed citation-shaped id" measurement was taken over the five rendered memos only, so it does not reach the imported-ledger documents this crate also checks, and on those the two matchers' merits are reversed. The claim holds as written only for ledgers whose ids are alphanumeric throughout, i.e. tetel-minted `C\d+`; it needs either a tokenisation that admits the crate's own id characters (alphanumeric, `_`, `-`, as scan_line already does inside brackets) or an explicit restriction of rule 5 to alphanumeric-id ledgers.

Everything but one number holds. Over the four other rendered memos in docs/design I replayed the corpus with the shipped `brief --json`: zero propositions of 61 contain a bracketed citation-shaped token, and real unbracketed same-ledger references exist in tet30 (C3 names C9 and C13). The clause that does not survive is the corpus size: "all five rendered memos — 90 claims". docs/design holds exactly five rendered memos, four of which carry 15+14+13+19 = 61 claims, and the fifth's own grounding brief announces 32 claims — 93, not 90. The figure looks measured against an earlier state of the fifth ledger (its ids run to C34 with two withdrawn). The qualitative findings the closure decision rests on are unaffected; the count is stale.

prop: Reusing `citation_ids_in` leaves one residual false negative — a proposition that names another claim in unbracketed prose, since `scan_line` begins an id scan only at a `[` byte — and this design states that as a bound rather than widening the matcher, because widening would create a second, disagreeing definition of the same citation edge for a check that already owns one.
note: The code states that `scan_line` recognizes bracketed `[ID]`/`[!ID]` forms and is shared by `citation_ids_in`, but it does not state that this leaves exactly one residual false negative or that widening was rejected to avoid a second citation-edge definition.

later.note: The false-negative class is real and correctly identified. The stated reason is one branch short: `scan_line` does not begin an id scan only at a `[` byte — it first calls `scan_cites_trailer`, which recognises a whole line of the form `*cites: C1, C4*` and returns unbracketed ids from it. That branch cannot rescue a proposition that merely names a claim in ordinary prose (the trailer must be the entire trimmed line), so the residual false negative stands as described; only the "only at a `[` byte" mechanism clause is inexact. Separately, `is_citation_shaped` also requires an id to contain a digit or a hyphen, so a bracketed id of a shape with neither would be a second, narrower residual miss.

The mechanism is exactly as described; "one residual false negative" understates it to the point of changing the decision. Measured over every memo this project has rendered — `brief --json` on all five, 90 claims — there are zero bracketed citation-shaped ids inside any proposition, and four bare unbracketed references (tet30 C3 -> C9/C13, tet30 C9 -> C99, tet47 C4 -> C5). The residual is not a corner: it is the whole observed population. Disjunct 4 of the decided predicate therefore contributes the empty edge set on every memo in this corpus, TET-47's own included, and the one real proposition-to-claim reference in TET-47's ledger is one of the four it does not see. That is the same shape of defect this memo used to kill rule 3 — a rule with no operand anywhere it would run — and it is stated here as a bound rather than recognised as one.

The proposition asserts that the residual false negative "is narrow and stated rather than closed", and states exactly one: a proposition referring to another claim by description rather than by id. There is a second, larger, unstated one that follows directly from the matcher's own tokenisation rule. Because the rule delimits tokens on punctuation and the hyphen is punctuation, a proposition that names a sibling *by its id* is still missed whenever that id contains a hyphen. src/citations.rs 38-55 gives the corpus-ledger id shape as uppercase-led with "a digit or a hyphen" (`S3-L17`, `E-4`, `X-6`, `R-ROOT`, `CYC-A`), and the captured rg sweep finds 21 hyphenated ledger row ids across nine fixture documents and two source modules with no unhyphenated one. src/ledger.rs 361-383 supplies the concrete case: claim `X-1`, proposition "`foo` returns **4** always [X-2]" — a by-id reference the matcher as worded does not see. So the missed-edge set is not narrow (it is every by-id reference on an entire class of ledgers this crate supports) and it is not stated. The error-direction half of the proposition — that a spurious edge only schedules an extra grading — is unaffected.

prop: Rule 5's fixpoint is a traversal of the reverse citation graph seeded with the claims owed by rules 1-4, and it terminates on any input — including a citation cycle — by the same `visited`-set construction check 5 already uses for row→row cascades; but the graph must be built over ledger claims, which check 5's `row_citers` deliberately excludes, so the construction is reused while the index itself is new.
note: The evidence supports reusing the visited-set BFS construction and shows that `row_citers` excludes ledger claims, requiring a new index. It does not establish that Rule 5's current fixpoint is already a traversal seeded by rules 1–4's owed ledger claims; the shown `analyze_ledger` logic is per-claim rather than graph-based.

prop: The confirmation floor and the designer's "stop after the first round that provokes no revision" rule do not conflict, because no rule in that stopping section makes the emptiness of any list a termination condition — the loop stops on machine-clean plus no refuted or unexplained claim, and the round-count rule keys on revisions provoked — so an owed list that is still non-empty at the stopping round is a schedule the run declines to spend another pass on, not an unmet exit criterion.
note: The evidence supports that human-owed items, including qualifications and non-coverage, need not be emptied before stopping, and that the no-revision rule prevents another pass. However, the stopping rule does require there to be no live refuted or unexplained claims, which is itself an emptiness condition for those categories, so “any list” is too broad.

prop: There should be no `--owed` flag: because the full brief is emitted either way, an owed section is purely additive and there is no prior behaviour a flag would preserve, while TET-46's stated objection to a flag — that it "leaves no trace in what the caller named, only in how they configured the call" — applies with more force to a brief, the one artifact independence rests on, since two passes running `brief` on the same memo would otherwise receive different documents; the confirmation floor stays a parameter, and the value in force is printed in the brief so that this piece of configuration does leave a trace in the artifact.
note: The evidence supports an unconditional brief containing every ledger claim and treats human-owed items as a separate non-failure partition, but the shown brief renderers do not print any confirmation-floor value. Thus the no-flag rationale is partly supported, while the claim that this configuration is traced in the artifact is not.

later.note: The no-flag decision stands; its closing remedy does not reach one of the two surfaces. "The value in force is printed in the brief so that this piece of configuration does leave a trace in the artifact" is met only for the text brief. `brief` already emits two documents from one memo depending on a flag the caller types: src/lib.rs 186-217 dispatches on `json` between `render_text` and `render_json` (src/brief.rs 36 and 62), reached by `--json` in src/main.rs 28-60 and main.rs:351. Since the design's own target list (C19) puts the owed section and the floor value in `render_text` only, a pass that runs `brief --json` receives a brief with neither — reinstating exactly the property this claim rejects a flag for, that the configuration leaves no trace in the artifact, and additionally making the two passes' briefs differ in content rather than in encoding. Also, this claim's premise that "two passes running `brief` on the same memo would otherwise receive different documents" is already true of `--json` today; the argument needs the stronger form that they must not receive different *content*, which is what the render_json omission breaks.
The TET-46 quotation is exact and correctly attributed as its objection to a flag.

"The full brief is emitted either way" rests on `build`'s unconditional one-for-one map and its doc comment forbidding any drop; and the two renderers are the two places a floor value would have to be printed, since neither prints any parameter today.

The TET-46 objection is quoted byte-exactly, including the "no flag" conclusion it supports. The rest of the proposition — that the full brief is emitted either way and no prior behaviour would be preserved by a flag, and that the floor stays a parameter printed by both renderers — rests on `build`'s unconditional map and the two-renderer shape I recorded separately; the printing requirement is a prescription, not yet code.

TET-46's objection is quoted accurately — docs/design/tet46-look-never-returns-tetel-content.md:85 reads "A flag would add a fourth route with a property none of these has — it leaves no trace in what the caller named, only in how they configured the call." That the full brief is emitted either way, so an owed section is purely additive with no prior behaviour to preserve, follows from `build`'s unconditional one-for-one mapping and its doc.

"Purely additive" is true only in the sense of removal, and the claim spends it in the stronger sense. The no-flag argument rests on "an owed section is purely additive and there is no prior behaviour a flag would preserve". There is prior behaviour: today's brief is evidence-blind by construction. `build` takes `&[Claim]` only and neither renderer emits a field derived from the evidence ledger, and brief.rs's module doc states this shape is a confidentiality device — scope is withheld "so an independent grounding pass can't see what the author declared", "enforced by its shape, not by care at render time" (F2). tests/brief_cli.rs states the reciprocal contract for evidence state in its own words: `brief` "must keep listing it exactly as if nothing had been recorded yet, until a witnessed grounding lands" (F3). An owed list is the first evidence-derived channel into that artifact: a grounder handed one learns, per claim, whether at least N independent workspaces have already graded the wording it is about to grade. That is prior behaviour a flag would preserve, and it is disclosure into the one artifact C16 itself calls "the one artifact independence rests on". The no-flag conclusion may still be right, but not on the ground that nothing is being given up.

The quoted objection is byte-exact against TET-46's prose at line 85 of that memo. Combined with brief.rs — where build emits every claim unconditionally and both renderers already print the whole list — the "no prior behaviour a flag would preserve" premise holds, and the reasoning that two passes must not receive different briefs is the same objection applied to the artifact independence rests on.

The no-flag decision holds only under a condition the claim does not state: that N is constrained to at least 1. C16 rejects `--owed` on the ground that "two passes running `brief` on the same memo must not receive different documents", then accepts the floor as a caller-supplied parameter. C24 states the predicate as an unqualified "owed iff fewer than N ..." with no lower bound, and C31 gives N a default without an admissible range. At N=0 no claim is ever owed on any memo — the owed section is empty — which is exactly the document a `--owed`-off flag would produce. So `brief --confirm 0` reinstates through the accepted parameter the artifact the claim rejects as a flag, and two passes at N=0 and N=2 do receive different documents from one memo. C28's separating argument ("a schedule and never a settlement") applies word for word to the flag, so it does not distinguish the two; and C16's other ground, TET-46's no-trace objection, is cured for N by printing the floor in force, a remedy that would equally cure it for the flag. The decision is defensible with "N >= 1" written into the predicate and rejected at both front ends; as the claim stands, that constraint is asserted nowhere in the ledger and assigned to nobody in the Modification targets table.

Everything but one clause holds: build takes &[Claim] alone (F4), build's own doc forbids dropping a claim on account of its evidence ledger, tests/brief_cli.rs carries the quoted sentence and asserts the ingested-only claim is still listed (F12), and TET-46's quoted sentence is verbatim at tet46 line 85 (F13). The clause I cannot support as written is "its module doc calls that shape a confidentiality device enforced by shape rather than by care", where "that shape" is `build` taking `&[Claim]` alone. The module doc's shape-enforcement sentence is attached to a different thing and to a different property: "`BriefItem` carries no field a scope could leak through — that's enforced by its shape, not by care at render time." That is about BriefItem's field list and about scope leakage, not about build's parameter list or about evidence-blindness. The evidence-blindness contract is stated in the code, but by build's own doc comment, not by the module doc's shape sentence.

The TET-46 quotation is byte-exact at that memo's line 85. The other checkable clauses hold too: build takes &[Claim] alone and its doc forbids dropping a claim on evidence grounds, the module doc's "enforced by its shape, not by care at render time" sentence is about BriefItem's field list and scope (F2), and brief_cli.rs carries the quoted "must keep listing it exactly as if nothing had been recorded yet, until a witnessed grounding lands" (F7). The N>=1 rejection is a design decision, not a code fact.

prop: Rule 4's visibility requirement is met by extending the existing per-claim provenance line in `grounding_provenance` with the number of distinct non-author workspaces that graded the claim's current wording, printed as a bullet in the human-owed partition exactly as that line already is; `check` states the count and never compares it against a floor, because the floor is `brief`'s parameter and a comparison printed by `check` would be a per-claim verdict on a policy setting rather than a count of records.
note: The evidence shows a human-owed bullet containing distinct witnessed workspace information and, when the author identity is known and the result is mixed, an explicit count of author versus non-author workspaces. It does not establish that every claim’s count is for the current wording or that the count is explicitly printed when all workspaces are independent, self-grounded, or the author identity is unavailable, nor does it show the asserted `brief`-floor behavior.

later.note: "The existing per-claim provenance line" is three different emission states, and the extension reaches only one of them — the one where the count is least likely to be zero. src/checks.rs 972-1050: when a claim has no evidence records at all, `grounding_provenance` does `continue` and emits NO line; when the witnessed subset is empty, it emits a different string ("grounded, all N record(s) ingested — extent typed by the reporter...") that carries no workspace list and no counts; only the third branch emits the "N of M record(s) witnessed in workspace(s) ..." line the claim proposes to extend, and the by_author/by_others split it would extend exists only inside `AuthoringIdentity::Known`. So a reader gets the new count exactly when a claim already has at least one witnessed record, and gets nothing where the count would be 0 — precisely the claims rule 4 schedules. The visibility requirement is met for grounded-and-witnessed claims only; the claim as written says it is met, without that condition. The rest of the claim — that `check` states the count and never compares it to N — is unaffected.

The mechanical half is confirmed: the provenance line is already emitted per grounded claim and already printed as a `  - ` bullet in report.rs's human-owed partition, so extending that same string with a count reaches the reader exactly as the proposition says. What I cannot establish from source is the normative half — that this "meets" rule 4's visibility requirement, and that `check` should state the count without comparing it to a floor. That is a design decision about a surface that does not exist yet; there is no code that states or fails to state it. Graded on the code half only.

The three-way split is correct on the axis it enumerates and incomplete on a second, independent one. src/checks.rs 940-1060: the outer branch is indeed three-way over record composition (no records -> `continue`; no witnessed records -> the all-ingested string; else the "N of M record(s) witnessed in workspace(s)" line). But inside the third branch `standing` switches on `AuthoringIdentity`, and `by_author`/`by_others` are computed only in the `Known(author)` arm — under `NoSnapshot` and `SnapshotWithoutIdentity` the function emits "cannot be determined from here" because there is no author to subtract. So "the count of distinct non-author workspaces that graded the wording a claim carries now" has no value to print in two of the three identity modes, and the instruction "It goes in all three" does not say what is emitted there. This is the same pair of states C10 keys the floor on, so it is not an edge case the design ignores elsewhere: C10 decides that in those states every claim is owed under rule 4, and C17 needs a matching decision about what the visibility line says — a count is not computable, and printing a bare zero would read as "no independent pass has graded this" when the truth is "nothing here can tell". Separately, emitting the count in the first branch means `grounding_provenance` now emits a line for claims with no evidence at all, which its own field doc describes as "one line per grounded claim" and which `analyze_ledger` already reports as ungrounded; the design should say whether that duplication is intended.

The "printed in the human-owed partition as its lines already are" clause: report.rs's loop over findings.grounding_provenance sits inside the human-owed block beside superseded_evidence and qualified_claims, one "  - {line}" per entry, never contributing to a failure.

The descriptive half is exact: the three composition states (no records → `continue`, emits nothing; all-ingested → a string with no workspace list; witnessed → the "N of M record(s) witnessed in workspace(s)" line), and within the third a second branch on AuthoringIdentity where a non-author count (`by_others`) is computed only in the `Known` arm, with NoSnapshot and SnapshotWithoutIdentity producing "cannot be determined from here" and no count. The remaining sentences are prescriptions for code that does not exist yet, so they are design decisions rather than facts of the tree; nothing I read contradicts them.

The description of the branching is exact — I read src/checks.rs 972-1050 and the three composition states and the `AuthoringIdentity` sub-branch are as stated, with `by_author`/`by_others` existing only in the `Known` arm. What does not hold is the completeness the proposition asserts for the purpose it uses the enumeration for: "the function branches on two axes, not one." There is a third, and it is the axis this design itself introduces. Every set the function builds — `records`, `witnessed`, `passes`, `by_author`, `by_others` — is selected by `claim_id` alone; `proposition_digest` is never read anywhere in the function. C9 requires the floor's count to be restricted to records matching the current wording, so the count and the sentence it is appended to would be computed over different record sets. Constructed case: a claim whose three witnessed records all graded a superseded wording, from three non-author workspaces. It lands in the third composition state, so the line prints "grounded, 3 of 3 record(s) witnessed in workspace(s) A, B, C — independently grounded: no grounding workspace here is the one that authored this memo", while the digest-restricted count appended to that same line is 0 and rule 4 schedules the claim. The `(0, _)` and `(_, 0)` arms produce "independently grounded" and "SELF-GROUNDED" from the unrestricted `passes` vector, so the standing verdict and the new count contradict each other on one line about one claim. This is the same trap one layer down from the one the claim credits itself with catching, and placing the count correctly requires the digest axis to be in the enumeration. Second, smaller: the instruction to emit the count in the first composition state turns a bare `continue` into a bullet for every claim with no evidence record — the population src/report.rs 179-200 already covers under "ungrounded ledger claims" in the same flat bullet list, so that state yields two bullets per claim, 32 of them on this memo's current ledger.

The two-axis structure is exactly as described. Composition axis: `records.is_empty()` continues without emitting; `witnessed.is_empty()` emits the all-ingested string with no workspace list; only the third branch carries "N of M record(s) witnessed in workspace(s)". Identity axis inside that third branch: `by_others` is computed only in the `Known(author)` arm, and the `NoSnapshot`/`SnapshotWithoutIdentity` arms produce a "cannot be determined from here" string with no count at all. src/report.rs:198 prints each of these lines verbatim as a bullet in the human-owed partition, which the section header says is "none of this is settled by a passing check", so the prescription that `check` state a count without comparing it to a floor is consistent with where the lines already land.

The two branch axes the claim enumerates are real and correctly described, and it misses a third that defeats the visibility requirement it is discharging. Inside `AuthoringIdentity::Known`, `grounding_provenance` branches again on `(by_author, by_others)` into three arms emitting three different verdict words — "independently grounded" at (0,_), "SELF-GROUNDED" at (_,0), "MIXED: {a} ... {o}" otherwise. All three are computed over `passes`, deduped from `witnessed` with NO digest filter, which is exactly the restriction C9 says the floor must add and this function does not have. So the claim's remedy puts a digest-AWARE count next to a digest-BLIND verdict word on the same line, and does not require the word to change. Replay of tet30's ledger: 125 records, 61 distinct pin values in that one file, and all 13 claims carry records with more than one distinct pin — C11 has 16, C10 and C12 have 8 each. The predicate does not say whether rule 3 fires when any, all, or the latest of a claim's record pins differs, and the three answers give different owed sets. (b) The comparison is between a per-fact `sha256:` content fingerprint (src/facts.rs 405-452) and a prose-parsed git token (src/ledger.rs 150-205), so no crate set is being reused here — unlike disjuncts 1, 2 and 4, this one is a new predicate over records, and it is the only disjunct with no existing computation behind it. Disjuncts 1, 2, 4 and 5 are unaffected by this record.

Four of the five disjuncts hold as stated and the closing summary is right for them. The third disjunct is not: "the pin stored on its records" is, on the witnessed path, `Some(fact.pin.clone())`, and a Fact's pin is `sha256:` + a hash over each extent entry's label, world_root, world_state and output (src/facts.rs:414-436) — never a VCS revision, whereas "the memo's currently stated pin" is a git hash parsed out of prose by `find_stated_pin` (the crate's own tests assert `abc1234` and `deadbee`). Compared directly, the two can never be equal, so this disjunct fires unconditionally on every witnessed-grounded claim rather than detecting a re-pin; the field that actually records the tree an observation was taken against is `world: Vec<worldstate::Marker>`, not `pin`. The final sentence is also over-broad on that disjunct: "each of the first four reuses a set the crate already computes" is true of rule 1 (`ungrounded_claims`), rule 2 (`out_of_proof`) and rule 4 (`by_others` inside `grounding_provenance`), but not of rule 3 — no check in the crate reads a record's pin at all (F5), so there is no computed set to reuse. "Every disjunct is decidable from the memo, its evidence file and its snapshot" is true as written (F7).

The condition C5 does not state, and needs: the zero-content state arises on a read whose selection BEGINS with the over-budget line — a ranged `look --lines k:…` with the long line at k (`--lines 15:20` on tet46, `--lines 2:2` on tet29). Under that condition the state is real and the floor is earned. As written, the claim's premise ("four tracked paths hold a long line") does not entail its conclusion ("that state is reachable" via the direct read it names), and the reader is left believing the plain read is the witness when it is not.

The rest of C5 — the line-boundary release rule, the character-boundary snap, the absence of any byte-safe cut in `src/`, the 1922 continuation bytes — is untouched by this.

Every measured component of C5 is exact — F3 reproduces all of them independently: exactly four tracked paths hold a line over 32768 bytes and all four are tetel's own .tetel/facts.jsonl ledgers, largest line 905745; the over-budget positions are 11 and 15 of 20, 15 of 21, 2 of 11, 2 of 10; a selection from line 1 releases 5, 2, 1 and 1 whole lines and never floors; the longest output line across the nine censuses is 1090 bytes; a whole-src grep for is_char_boundary/char_indices/.truncate( returns no matches; the longest single line carries 1922 UTF-8 continuation bytes. The grep line shape and the split unit are as stated.

The qualification is one clause: "`look_path` refuses only a missing path and a directory". look_path has THREE `workspace::refuse` sites, not two — the third is `invalid --lines range {a}:{b}` at src/observe.rs:300-302, fired when `a < 1 || a > b`. The "only" is false as written. It does not disturb the conclusion drawn from it (each of the four ledgers is readable directly, and the exclusion-filtering half of the clause is correct — look_path calls no Exclusions::decide and filters nothing), but the third refusal sits inside the very `match lines` block C20 instructs an implementer to restructure, so an implementer told there are only two refusals there is misinformed about the code they are about to edit.

prop: The bound cannot be derived from the caller's cap: the MCP `look` handler receives no field carrying one and returns `printed` unmeasured, so any number tetel applies is chosen by a person. Following this crate's own handling of an arbitrary number — `describe_buffer`, which refuses to invent a staleness threshold on the grounds that "a number chosen here would be arbitrary" and reports instead — the constant must be documented as a judgement and the design's load must rest on the report, not on the number.
note: The evidence supports that `look` passes only its path/line or grep inputs to `observe::dispatch` and returns `outcome.printed`, and that `describe_buffer` reports age without an arbitrary staleness cutoff. It does not itself establish the prescriptive conclusion that the constant must be documented as a judgement or that the design must rely on the report rather than the number.

later.note: LookParams (mcp.rs:212-227) has only workspace/path/lines/grep — no cap field of any kind — and the handler at mcp.rs:644 is `text_result(outcome.printed)` with no length measurement. The precedent is quoted correctly: describe_buffer's doc comment reads "a number chosen here would be arbitrary" and the function reports the buffer's ages instead of enforcing a threshold.

prop: Nothing in this crate's source truncates anything today — a whole-`src` grep for `truncat` finds only one doc comment, about acknowledgements being untruncatable — so f3 introduces a new behaviour rather than moving an existing one, and there is no in-crate convention for how a truncation should be spelled.
note: The evidence supports that a whole-`src` search for `truncat` found one match, in a comment saying the acknowledgement cannot be truncated. It does not establish that nothing truncates by other wording, that f3 is wholly new rather than moved, or that no convention exists for spelling truncation.

later.note: Counterexample on the axis the evidence never searched. `transplants::refuse_incomplete` (transplants.rs 428-440) truncates a premise's text to its first line before showing it to the author and marks the cut with a trailing ` …`. That is a truncation in this crate's source today, released at a line boundary, in text the author reads — so both halves of C7 fail: it is not true that "nothing in this crate's source truncates anything today", and it is not true that "there is no in-crate convention for how a truncation should be spelled". F8's grep for the word `truncat` could not have found it, because the code never uses that word; the claim rests on a name search standing in for a behaviour search. The design consequence is small but real: an in-crate spelling exists and f3's label segment departs from it (it reports how much was withheld, which the transplant elision does not), and the memo asserts there was nothing to depart from, so the departure is never argued.

The citation is exact — transplants.rs:432-435 is the loop that takes `text.lines().next()`, appends ` …` only under `text.lines().count() > 1`, and pushes the result. Cut on a line boundary: yes. Marker only when lines were dropped: yes (a single-line premise gets `first.to_string()` with no marker). No count of what was dropped anywhere in `shown` or `msg`: confirmed. The whole-src grep for `truncat` returning only a doc comment is also confirmed at this HEAD.
Confirms the second half: the single `truncat` hit in src is acks.rs:25, a `//!` doc comment about the ack log being monotone, not a truncation implementation.

prop: This design recommends 32768 bytes (32 KiB) as the bound, declared in the source as a judgement and not as a measurement. Its only stated constraint is that it be strictly below whatever cap the caller applies, and since tetel cannot observe that cap the value is chosen conservatively; its consequence on the nine censuses measured here is that seven of them (claim, fact, check, prose, ack, render, get) return bounded and two (target at 24974 bytes, label at 8201) return whole.
note: The census does support that target (24,974 bytes) and label (8,201 bytes) are below 32 KiB, while the other seven exceed it. However, the shown grep path returns the full stdout, and those seven outputs are 45,210–162,896 bytes, so the evidence does not show them actually returning bounded results at 32 KiB.

later.note: The consequence is reproduced with margin. Rebuilding look_grep's exact grep invocation, the seven censuses claim/fact/check/prose/ack/render/get come to 162183/124840/123826/81081/74680/61431/44497 bytes of stdout alone, every one far above 32768; target and label come to 24261 and 7488 bytes of stdout, and to 24975 and 8202 as full returns (stdout plus the `({note})\n` exclusion line, whose byte-exact reconstruction is 714 with the six-memo list that predates this memo's own .md). The stated 24974 and 8201 are exactly those returns less the trailing newline, so both figures are reproducible under a stated convention. Worth knowing, not a defect: these two numbers embed the exclusion note, which lists rendered memo paths, so they drift as memos are added — the seven-bounded/two-whole conclusion does not.

prop: The plain `look <path>` and `look --lines A:B` paths must be left alone by this design, because in `look_path` the returned bytes and the captured `output` are the same value `shown`; bounding the return there would necessarily change what is captured, which the ticket puts out of scope. `look_grep` is bounded and `look_path` is not, and that asymmetry is a consequence of the code's shape, not an oversight.
note: The code does show that `PendingEntry.output` is `shown`, but `look_path` returns `printed`, which also includes a header and sometimes a trailing newline, so the returned value and captured output are not the same value. The evidence also does not establish that the ticket puts bounding `look_path` out of scope or that the asymmetry is intentional rather than an oversight.

later.note: The claim's premise is right and its inference is false. In `look_path` (observe.rs 268-336) `printed` is a separate String assembled by `printed.push_str(&shown)` at line 316 — a byte copy — and `shown` is moved into `PendingEntry.output` afterwards at line 325. Two independent Strings exist between those points, which is the same separation `look_grep` exploits. Bounding `printed` after line 316 would therefore NOT "necessarily change what is captured": the capture would be byte-identical, exactly as C2 says it is on the grep path. So the asymmetry is not "a consequence of the code's shape"; it is a choice the design is entitled to make but has not justified. This matters because C9 is an instruction to an implementer — it tells them the `look <path>` case is closed by construction, which suppresses the observation that after f3 ships, `look <path>` on a large file is still silently cut by the caller with no trace anywhere, the very defect the ticket names.

The cited range is exact: observe.rs:314-330 is `let mut printed = String::new();` … `printed.push_str(&shown);` … then `PendingEntry { … output: shown, … }`. `shown` is copied into `printed` by borrow and only moved into the entry afterwards, so the two strings are independent and a bound on `printed` cannot reach the captured output, label or key.

prop: `look --lines` already contains this design's pattern in miniature: when the requested range runs past the end of the file the label records what was actually delivered rather than what was asked (`lines {a}-{end}` with `end = b.min(total)`, or an explicit "nothing in range" for an empty result), so recording a shortfall in the observation label is an established convention in this module rather than a new invention.
note: The `look_path` implementation labels a truncated range as `lines {a}-{end}` with `end = b.min(total)`, and labels an entirely out-of-range request with an explicit “nothing in range” note. This directly establishes the claimed shortfall-recording convention in the module.

later.note: observe.rs:296-313 is verbatim what the claim quotes: `let end = b.min(total);` with label `{path} lines {a}-{end}`, and the a>total branch labelling `{path} lines {a}-{b} (file has {total} line(s); nothing in range)`. The label therefore states the delivered range, not the requested one, so annotating a shortfall in the observation label already exists in this module.

prop: `look_grep` is the only function this design changes, and the change is contained: a whole-worktree census finds it in two files — the definition at src/observe.rs:349 and the one call site in `dispatch` at observe.rs:506, the remaining three occurrences being doc comments. Because the bound and the label are both assembled inside the function and its signature is unchanged, no caller has to be touched.
note: The census supports two files, the definition and dispatch call site, plus three doc-comment occurrences. But it does not establish that no other function was changed or that the signature is unchanged relative to the prior design, so the “only” and “no caller has to be touched” clauses are not settled.

later.note: Every number checks out on this HEAD: look_grep occurs five times across src/observe.rs and src/worldstate.rs — definition at observe.rs:349, the single dispatch call at observe.rs:506, doc mentions at observe.rs:76, observe.rs:495 and worldstate.rs:76; look_path four times in src/observe.rs alone — definition 277, dispatch call 516, doc mentions 4 and 495. No test file, no binary and no other module names either. One point of care rather than a qualification: a raw whole-worktree grep also matches rendered memos, `.evidence.jsonl` files and `.tetel/` ledgers, which is exactly the tetel-output class a census withholds, so "five times in two files" is the census's count, not the raw grep's.

prop: A bounded return changes nothing about what TET-28's census refusal guarantees, and its refusal text needs no change. The refusal fires on `ExtentEntry::censuses`, which reads the search's existence and its root out of an immutable extent that a bound applied to `printed` does not touch; and the text already disclaims the reading a bounded return would threaten, saying the refusal "is about the search's existence and where it was rooted, never about what it found".
note: The evidence shows the refusal checks whether the immutable fact extent contains a census entry, while the grep search records existence and root independently of the `printed` output. The existing refusal text explicitly says it concerns the search’s existence and root, not what it found.

later.note: `ExtentEntry::censuses` reads only kind, pattern, world_root and key from the extent — never the returned text — and the target refusal fires on `fact.extent.iter().any(|e| e.censuses(symbol))`, so a bound on `printed` cannot change whether it fires. The refusal text at targets.rs:171 already ends "The refusal is about the search's existence and where it was rooted, never about what it found", which is exactly the disclaimer a bounded return would otherwise need added.

prop: Hitting the bound must not be an error at the destination: `look_grep` returns the bounded text as a successful `LookOutcome` exactly as it returns a whole one, and records the shortfall in the label rather than refusing. This follows the crate's own report-rather-than-refuse handling of an arbitrary number in `describe_buffer`, and it is forced anyway — the pending entries are already written from the full stdout by the time any bound is applied, so a refusal would have to discard a capture that already happened.
note: The evidence shows `look_grep` captures and returns full `stdout` and its labels record matches and exclusions, but it does not show any bound being applied or a shortfall label. `describe_buffer` supports the report-rather-than-refuse analogy, yet it does not establish the claimed bounded-`look_grep` behavior or that refusal would necessarily occur after persistence.

later.note: The first two sentences hold: look_grep's only success path is `Ok(LookOutcome { printed })`, there is no error return keyed to result size, and the label is the natural place for the shortfall. The final clause — "it is forced anyway — the pending entries are already written from the full stdout by the time any bound is applied, so a refusal would have to discard a capture that already happened" — is not what observe.rs:415-479 shows. On the match branch `printed.push_str(&stdout)` runs *first*, before `by_file` is built and before any PendingEntry is constructed; and `pending::save(workspace_dir, &buf)?` is the last statement before the `Ok`. So an implementation bounding while assembling `printed` (which is how C2 describes it) reaches the bound before the entries exist and before anything is persisted, and could return `Err` without discarding any capture. Report-rather-than-refuse is a good choice here, but it is a choice, not something the code's ordering forces.

I read every `workspace::refuse` site the crate-wide sweep found (F3 for the sweep, F7 for the texts): all are missing/malformed input, a nonexistent or withdrawn referent, a forbidden flag combination, or a provenance/precondition failure with a singular remedy. None is conditioned on a measurement of a result. The ordering claim (`printed.push_str(&stdout)` before `by_file` and before any PendingEntry; `pending::save` the last statement before `Ok`) is F2; the targets.rs discriminator text and the census refusal wording are F5; describe_buffer's "a number chosen here would be arbitrary" is F4.

prop: The bound cannot disturb observation identity at the destination: the `Search` entry is keyed by `search_key(root_path, &m.root)` and each per-file entry by `resolve_key(Path::new(&file))`, both computed from paths alone, so two searches of the same root for the same pattern overlap each other whether either was bounded or not.
note: The code keys the whole-search record from `root_path` and the world root derived for that path, and keys each file record from the reported file path; neither key includes the bound or exclusion state. Thus identical roots and matching files use the same observation identities regardless of whether the search was bounded.

later.note: Both key functions take only paths: resolve_key is fs::canonicalize with a path fallback, search_key resolves the root and picks between that spelling and the world root by canonical equality. Neither reads the pattern or any part of stdout, and the call sites in look_grep are exactly search_key(root_path, &m.root) for the Search entry and resolve_key(Path::new(&file)) per matched file, so a bound on printed cannot move a key.

prop: The bound earns its own `NON_COVERAGE` line rather than being folded into an existing one. The list already discriminates a withholding tetel chose (the tetel-output exclusion) from platform accidents that "contemplate nothing tetel chose" (grep skipping symlinked directories and binary files); a bound tetel applies to its own return is of the first kind. What the line states is a gap `check` genuinely cannot close: a fact's extent records the whole search, and nothing anywhere establishes that the author read all of it — `scope.rs` names that limit as permanently out of reach and does not claim otherwise.
note: The evidence explicitly separates the platform-skipping entry from the separate tetel-output exclusion and states that tetel’s own non-coverage is independently listed. `scope.rs` also expressly limits the check to captured extent versus authored notes and says truth or sincere examination is permanently out of reach.

later.note: The NON_COVERAGE list does make the discrimination the claim relies on, in the source comment's own words: the symlink/binary entry "names two *platform accidents* and contemplates nothing tetel chose", and the tetel-output exclusion is kept as "A separate line, deliberately not folded into the one above… A deliberate exclusion earns its own line, by the same standard as every other entry here." A bound tetel applies to its own return is a deliberate withholding, so by that stated standard it earns its own line.

The second half holds too: nothing in the tool establishes that an author examined what an extent records, and scope.rs's module doc registers exactly that as out of reach — "Whether the note is *correct* about the location it names is exactly the limit this project registered as permanently out of reach ('insincere examination' — capture makes the extent honest, not the interpretation). Nothing here touches that." It states the limit rather than claiming coverage of it.

This claim instructs an implementer what a declared modification target (`NON_COVERAGE`) must say, and what it specifies is census-shaped while the design is not. Its content sentence is "a fact's extent records the whole search, and nothing anywhere establishes that the author read all of it", and the prose spends it the same way ("the list carries the general statement that a census's return to its author is bounded"), as does C16 ("the static list says a census reports the tree minus what tetel withheld"). But C9 and C20 put `look_path` inside the same bound, and F1(4) confirms a plain `look <path>` is a wholly different act — no search, no root, no exclusions, an extent naming one file and a range. An implementer who writes the line this claim specifies leaves every bounded path read with no standing statement anywhere in `check`'s non-coverage list, which is the one surface the design nominates for the general case. The single-line decision may well still be right, but the line has to be written for both acts — "what `look` returns to its author is bounded, and nothing establishes the author read the whole of what the extent records" — not for a census. As it stands the claim's own wording, followed literally, produces a line that covers `look_grep` only.

report.rs:86-190 carries both entries and the comment between them verbatim: the platform-accident entry ("symlinked directories and binary files"), the tetel-output entry, and "A deliberate exclusion earns its own line, by the same standard as every other entry here". No entry in the list concerns what `look` returned to its author. `look_path` applying no exclusion filtering is F2 and is also stated in the tetel-output entry itself; scope.rs naming interpretation/insincere examination as permanently out of reach is F5.

The claim's own generalising argument does not stop where the claim stops it, and the standing line it specifies will mislead by contrast.

C15 argues correctly that a `NON_COVERAGE` line phrased about a search "would leave every bounded path read with no standing statement anywhere in the list, which is the one surface this design nominates for the general case", and concludes the line must say: "what `look` returned to its author is bounded, and a fact's extent records the whole of what was observed while nothing establishes that the author was shown all of it."

Run that argument one step further. `look` is not the only verb that writes an observation into the pending buffer and hands its author a return the caller then cuts. `run` does the same: `run_command` captures the child's merged stdout/stderr, pushes a `Proc` PendingEntry whose `output` is that capture, and returns it whole and unmeasured; both front ends hand it straight back with no size check — `print!("{}", outcome.printed)` at src/main.rs:526 and `"output": outcome.printed` at src/mcp.rs:653-656 (F3). The `run` tool's own description at src/mcp.rs:649 documents the large case explicitly ("a command whose output is enormous … puts that in a repository forever"). So a `run` observation has precisely the defect this design exists to remove — the coupling between what was captured and what the author saw is broken by the caller, silently — and after f3 it is not merely unfixed but affirmatively contrasted against, because the new standing line names `look`.

The condition C15 does not state: its second half — "a fact's extent records the whole of what was observed while nothing establishes that the author was shown all of it" — is true of every fact in the ledger regardless of which verb captured it, but the line as specified scopes it to `look`. A reader of `check`'s standing non-coverage will reasonably infer the caveat does not apply to `run`-captured facts, which is exactly backwards: those are the ones with no bound, no shortfall segment and no trace at all.

Not a demand that f3 bound `run` — that is a scoping decision the design may keep. What is owed is either a line whose general half is not verb-scoped, or a stated reason why `run` is excluded from a statement the design itself calls the general case.

The verifiable parts hold. The standing list does discriminate a chosen withholding from platform accidents, and its comment says verbatim "A deliberate exclusion earns its own line, by the same standard as every other entry here", beside the entry naming grep skipping symlinked directories and binary files. The first half's factual load is correct: `run_command` returns the child's whole captured output unmeasured with no length test anywhere in the function, and both front ends hand it back whole (`print!("{}", outcome.printed)` in main.rs's Run arm; `"output": outcome.printed` in the MCP run tool); the run tool's own description does contemplate "a command whose output is enormous" and answers by warning rather than bounding. `look_path` applies no exclusion filtering at all.

The qualification is the clause "`scope.rs` names that second half as permanently out of reach". The only occurrence of "permanently out of reach" in the whole of src/ is src/scope.rs:42, and what it registers there is a different proposition: "Whether the note is *correct* about the location it names is exactly the limit this project registered as permanently out of reach (\"insincere examination\" — capture makes the extent honest, not the interpretation)." That is about the truth of an author's interpretation of a location, not about how much of a capture the author was shown. Reading it as naming the second half ("a fact's extent records the whole of what was observed, and nothing establishes that the author was shown all of it") requires stretching "insincere examination" from not-examined to not-shown, and scope.rs does not spell that out. This matters because it is the clause carrying the memo's assurance that the new entry "names an old limit that had been invisible rather than admitting a new weakness" — after the bound, `look` genuinely shows the author less than the extent records, which is new. Separate, non-blocking: the list itself is `NON_COVERAGE` in src/report.rs:86, not in scope.rs; C15 does not misattribute it, but the two files are easy to conflate here.

prop: The `NON_COVERAGE` entry must carry the general statement only, with the per-search numbers left to the label, because every string in that list is static and none is per-search. This is exactly the division TET-46 already made for exclusions: the static list says a census reports the tree minus what tetel withheld, and each search's own label names what that particular search withheld, which is what a reader of the Facts table sees.
note: The evidence explicitly states that every `NON_COVERAGE` string is static and that per-search exclusions belong in each search record’s label. The `look_grep` implementation constructs the exclusion note and includes it in the recorded label, matching the claimed division.

later.note: `NON_COVERAGE` is a `const &[&str]` of string literals only — nothing per-search can be placed there — and the source comment says so in the same words the claim uses ("every string in this list is static and none is per-search"). The TET-46 division is also literally present: the list entry says "a census reports the tree minus what tetel previously wrote into it. Each search's own record names the exclusions it was given", and the comment adds that the per-search set is written into the search record's own label "where a reader of the Facts table sees exactly which paths a given search withheld".

`const NON_COVERAGE: &[&str]` (report.rs:86-190) holds nothing but string literals, so no entry can be per-search; the comment states exactly that and draws exactly the split the claim describes, and the tetel-output entry pairs "a census reports the tree minus what tetel previously wrote into it" with "Each search's own record names the exclusions it was given". The Facts table rendering labels is F4; the `Path` label carrying its own per-observation text is F2.

prop: The label's unit is matching lines, and the proposed spelling inserts one segment into the existing `Search` label when and only when the bound was reached — schematically `search: <root> (grep: check) — 71 files matched — showed N of 883 matching lines (32768-byte bound) — <exclusion note>`, where 71 and 883 are this HEAD's measured values for that census and N is whatever the bound admitted. Matching lines is the right unit because it is what grep emits and what `look_grep` splits on; the existing matched-file count is computed from the full stdout and so stays true even when the return is bounded; and an unbounded search gains no segment at all, absence meaning whole, which is how `look --lines` already annotates a range only when it was clamped.
note: No evidence was provided, so the claim's specific assertions about the label unit, measured counts, bounding behavior, and annotation convention cannot be established.

later.note: The design content is right — matching lines is what grep emits and what look_grep splits on; `files` is `by_file.len()` computed from the full stdout and so survives a bound on `printed`; and an unbounded search gaining no segment matches how `--lines` annotates only a clamped range. The clause that fails is "where 71 and 883 are this HEAD's measured values for that census". At HEAD 81137aa the `check` census matches 883 lines (correct) across **70** files, not 71 — counted both by `grep -l` and by the distinct first-colon fields of the `-n -H` output, which is exactly how `by_file.len()` is computed. Since a matched file contributes at least one line, 71 files and 883 lines cannot both be this HEAD's values.

The numbers and the unit are confirmed independently (F6): reproducing look_grep's own exclusion set and running the grep gives exactly 883 matching lines and 70 distinct first-colon fields, and appending one trailing parenthesised exclusion-note line raises the distinct-field count to 71, which is the stated cause of the earlier figure. `by_file.len()` is indeed the count of distinct first-colon fields and is computed from the full stdout (F2), and `stdout.lines()` is what look_grep splits on. The clause that does not hold as written is the closing analogy, "which is how `look --lines` already annotates a range only when it was clamped": look_path writes `{path} lines {a}-{end}` into the label on every ranged read, clamped or not (observe.rs:308-309), so the range annotation is not clamp-conditional. What is conditional is only the empty-selection form `{path} lines {a}-{b} (file has {total} line(s); nothing in range)`. The analogy therefore overstates the existing convention; the proposed "absence means whole" behaviour for the shortfall segment is not itself in question.

prop: There is no act that gets an author the rest of a bounded census, and this design does not add one. Narrowing the root or the pattern is not available as a remedy, because a census is "one search of the whole worktree for the symbol itself" and a narrowed search stops qualifying as one; `look --grep` takes no other parameter that could page or filter. What remains available is an additional search rooted at a subdirectory, recorded as its own observation alongside the census rather than in place of it — and, outside the return path entirely, the per-file `GrepMatch` entries, which hold every matched line and ship complete into the snapshot.
note: The refusal defines a census as one workspace-rooted search for the symbol itself, while `look --grep` accepts only the pattern and root and records a subdirectory search as a separate observation. The implementation also stores each file’s complete matched-line output in `GrepMatch` entries that are persisted into the snapshot.

later.note: The escape hatch the claim points at is real: mint stores every non-empty pending output in full into the fact, and that facts.jsonl ships in the snapshot beside the memo, so the per-file GrepMatch entries — which hold every matched line — are recoverable there even when the return was cut. The census-narrowing half is settled by the target refusal's own words ("a census is one search of the whole worktree for the symbol itself") together with `censuses` requiring key == world_root, so a subdirectory-rooted search cannot qualify; and `look --grep` takes no paging or filtering parameter — LookParams is workspace/path/grep/lines, and lines is refused outright when combined with grep. Re-reading a bounded plain `look <path>` with `--lines A:B` keys on resolve_key(p) regardless of range, so it overlaps the first read.

The `look_path` half of this claim — "`--lines A:B` is already a first-class parameter of the same verb, so the author reads the rest of the file by asking for it" — is broken by a state reachable on tracked files in this worktree.

Construction. Take `look /Volumes/SSD/Documents/lonic/tetel/docs/design/tet46-look-never-returns-tetel-content.md.tetel/facts.jsonl`. F1(7) measures it: 20 lines, of which two exceed 32768 bytes, the longest 905745. F1(4) confirms `look_path` applies no exclusion filtering of any kind, so a named snapshot path is read like any other file — nothing stops this call. Under the rule the design states ("accumulate whole lines, and stop before the first line that would carry the total past the byte budget", C5/C20), the return stops at whichever over-budget line comes first. The author then asks for the rest with `--lines k:20`. The selection now BEGINS with a 905745-byte line, no whole line fits under 32768, and the bound admits zero lines: the author gets the `==> path <==` header, an empty body, and a label reading "showed 0 of N lines (32768-byte bound)". Every range that includes that line behaves identically. There is no `--lines` argument that returns any byte of it, so the claim's remedy does not reach it, and "needs nothing new either" is false: this case needs something the design does not have (a floor of one line, a byte-level fallback for an over-budget line, or at minimum an explicit statement that an over-budget line is unreadable through `look`).

Worse than the status quo on exactly the axis the ticket cares about. Today the caller truncates at ~59 KB, so the author reading that file sees its first ~59 KB. Under the design they see zero bytes of that line. The memo's answer to "what does an author do" is that the design "does not give the author back what was withheld; it stops the withholding from being secret" — but here the design withholds strictly more than the status quo did, and this claim asserts a remedy that does not exist.

The same construction reaches `look_grep`: a grep whose matching line is one of these long JSON lines emits a `<file>:<lineno>:<text>` line over the budget, and if it is the first matching line the bounded return is empty while the label still says "N files matched". The prose's consolation that "even a heavily bounded return still tells the author truthfully how many files matched" is then a file count attached to nothing.

The CLI `Look` command has exactly `path`, `--lines A:B` and `--grep PATTERN` — no paging, offset, limit or filtering parameter — and the MCP handler takes the same three plus `workspace` (F5). The census definition "a census is one search of the whole worktree for the symbol itself" is verbatim at targets.rs:168 (F5). GrepMatch entries holding every matched line, and the `Path` entry's output being the complete selected text with the key resolved before any range handling, are F2; facts.jsonl shipping as the first SNAPSHOT_FILES entry is F4.

C18's universal about the residue is false as written, and the true version is a worse residue than the one stated. The claim says: "What `--lines` does not reach is a single line longer than the budget: on such a line every range containing it returns the same floor — its first bytes up to a character boundary at or below 32768 — and no argument to `look` returns the remainder."

Constructed counterexample from the measured line lengths (F1). Take tet46 …/facts.jsonl: 20 lines, with 905745 bytes at line 15 and lines 12/13/14 at 4585/4320/2945 bytes. Ask `--lines 12:20`. That range contains line 15. Under C5's release rule the selection accumulates lines 12, 13 and 14 (11853 bytes with newlines), then stops before line 15 because it would carry the total past 32768. A whole line fitted, so the floor does not fire. The return contains zero bytes of line 15 and is not "the same floor".

The condition C18 does not state: the floor is returned only by a range that BEGINS at the over-budget line. Every other range containing it returns none of it. So the author's recovery act is not "ask for a range containing it" but "ask for a range starting exactly at it" — and to know which k that is, they must already know where the long line sits, which the bounded return does not tell them (the label reports N of M, not which line overran). The residue is therefore larger than C18 states: not merely "the remainder of that line is unreachable", but "the floored prefix itself is reachable only from one specific range start, discoverable only by bisection".

The claim's headline — that no act gets the author the rest of a bounded return, and that the escape hatch is the fact's captured `output` in the snapshot — is unaffected.

The measurements are exact. Simulating the release rule under 32768 bytes on the tet46 …/facts.jsonl ledger: `--lines 12:20` releases lines 12-14 at 11852 bytes and no byte of line 15; `--lines 8:20` releases three whole lines (8-10) and no byte of line 11. The census remedies are closed as stated: src/targets.rs carries verbatim "a census is one search of the whole worktree for the symbol itself", and `look --grep` takes no paging or filtering parameter — `LookParams` (src/mcp.rs:211-227) has exactly workspace/path/lines/grep, and the CLI reaches look_grep through `LookRequest::Grep { pattern, root }` with nothing further. The per-file GrepMatch entries hold every matched line and facts.jsonl is the first entry of SNAPSHOT_FILES.

The qualification is the clause "but never which line of the selection overran". On a floored return C20 fixes the label as `<path> lines {a}-{end} — showed 0 of M lines; first line cut mid-line at B of L bytes (32768-byte bound)`. "first line" names which line of the selection overran, and combined with the `lines {a}-{end}` segment it names the file line too (it is a). So the "never" is over-strong for exactly the case the same sentence has just described. The claim's substance survives: on a bounded but unfloored return — the case the bisection argument is about — the label reports only how many whole lines were shown and does not say the next one was over budget rather than merely not fitting, so the position is not recoverable from it and bisection is the honest description.

Full stdout is reconstructible byte-for-byte, and the design's own label states the budget it applied, so replaying the release rule reproduces N exactly. What C19 asserts is unrecoverable is recoverable in this mode. The claim's conclusion survives untouched, because the two grounds it states for `look_path` — that a replay answers what today's build would show rather than what this author was shown, and that a label's audience holds a rendered memo with no captured output in front of them — apply verbatim to a single-file grep. Read directly in src/observe.rs. Recursive mode: the Search entry's `output` is `String::new()`, and the per-file entries are collected into `by_file: BTreeMap<String, Vec<String>>` keyed by filename, so grep's stdout order — the order a bound would consume — is not in the ledger. For look_path, `PendingEntry { output: shown, .. }` receives the complete selection.

The three supporting facts outside observe.rs all check. prop: The `prose-revised-since-proof` listing is a pure function of three recomputed quantities and stores none of them: a block's current (text, cite-list) pair, the timestamp at which that exact pair first appeared in the block's event history, and an anchor equal to the maximum over the block's cited claims of each claim's earliest non-refuting record whose proposition digest matches the claim's current wording. The block is listed exactly when the pair's first-appearance timestamp exceeds the anchor, and is skipped outright when it is a heading, when its current cite-list is empty, or when no cited claim has such a record.
note: The selection rule is supported: the function recomputes the current pair, earliest matching non-refuting proof times, and the maximum anchor, with the stated skip gates and comparison. However, its returned `ProseRevisedSinceProof` stores `block_timestamp` and `cited` proof timestamps, so the claim that it stores none of these quantities is too strong.

later.note: checks.rs:414-557 states each element: first_proof per claim = earliest non-Refutes record whose proposition_digest equals sha256 of the claim's current proposition; anchor = max of those over the block's cited claims; block_timestamp = min timestamp among versions whose (text, cite) both equal the current pair; push iff block_timestamp > anchor; `continue` on heading, on empty current cite-list, and on the existential gate (no cited claim in first_proof). All recomputed per call from prose_events/claims/evidence; nothing derived is persisted.

`prose_after_proof` takes exactly (prose_events, claims, evidence) and recomputes all three quantities in-body: the current (text, cite) pair from the replayed history, the min timestamp over versions whose text AND cite both equal the current pair, and `anchor = max` over cited claims of the earliest record whose `proposition_digest == sha256_hex(claim.proposition)` and whose verdict is not `Refutes`. Pushes iff `block_timestamp > anchor`; `continue`s on `h.heading`, on `cur_cite.is_empty()`, and on `cited.is_empty()` (the existential gate). Nothing is persisted.

prop: The acknowledgement event cannot live in `prose.jsonl`. `ProseEvent` is an internally-tagged serde enum over exactly `Create` and `Revise`, and `workspace::read_jsonl` propagates any line's parse failure as an error over the whole log rather than skipping it; empirically, a build at this pin reading a `prose.jsonl` containing one valid `Create` line and one `{"event":"Ack",...}` line fails the entire read with `unknown variant \`Ack\`, expected \`Create\` or \`Revise\`` and exits 1. A new tag value therefore makes every older build unable to read even the prose it already understood.

The captured run with a valid `Create` followed by `Ack` produced the stated unknown-variant error and exited 1, establishing that the unknown tag prevents the log from being read.
