prop: A sibling `acks.jsonl`, added to `snapshot::SNAPSHOT_FILES`, degrades safely in the older build it will be shipped past: that constant is an explicit enumeration whose stated purpose is that a future workspace file be a deliberate decision to ship or withhold, so a build that predates the entry simply never opens the file, reads `prose.jsonl` unchanged, and reproduces TET-30's un-suppressed listing. The failure direction is therefore over-reporting a residue entry a newer build would suppress, never suppressing one an older build would show.
note: The evidence supports that `SNAPSHOT_FILES` is an explicit, non-wholesale enumeration and that prose loading reads `prose.jsonl`, but it does not establish that `acks.jsonl` has been added or that every older-build code path never opens it. It also does not directly show TET-30’s listing or prove the absolute “never suppressing” failure-direction claim.

later.note: C4's dominance sentence — "The failure direction is therefore over-reporting a residue entry a newer build would suppress, never suppressing one an older build would show" — is refuted by construction. It reasons only about the READ side (an old build never opens acks.jsonl). The WRITE side breaks it. `snapshot::write` (src/snapshot.rs:135-146) copies `SNAPSHOT_FILES` and never removes anything already in `<memo>.tetel/`, and skips any entry absent from the workspace. `SNAPSHOT_FILES` is a per-build constant. Construction: (1) author acks block P in workspace W with a new build and runs `render --out` — the snapshot now holds acks.jsonl = [Ack(P, key k)]; (2) author reconsiders and appends `Unack(P)`, so W's log is [Ack, Unack] and P must list again; (3) the memo is re-rendered by a build predating the SNAPSHOT_FILES entry — exactly "the older build it will be shipped past" that C4 posits. That build refreshes prose.jsonl, claims.jsonl and the memo bytes, and leaves the stale acks.jsonl in place because it does not know the name. (4) A newer build's `check` reads `snapshot_dir/acks.jsonl` (src/lib.rs:150-211 shows every residue input comes from the snapshot dir), finds [Ack] with key k still matching the recomputed text/cites/digests, and suppresses P — an entry both the older build and the true workspace state say should be shown. Nothing reddens: `compose::render` (src/compose.rs:79-95) reads only prose/claims/targets/transplants/facts, so acks.jsonl is outside the provenance-drift comparison by design (C13). The same state is reachable with a single build and no mixed builds at all, via the documented "A file absent from the workspace is skipped rather than erroring" path: render once from a workspace holding an ack, then re-render after that workspace's acks.jsonl is gone (restored/rebuilt workspace), and the stale ack keeps suppressing.

Nothing in snapshot.rs, compose.rs or lib.rs enumerates the snapshot directory (no fs::read_dir outside observe.rs/scope.rs/workspace.rs), and compose::render reads only the five named logs, so a build predating the entry never opens acks.jsonl and reads prose.jsonl unchanged. SNAPSHOT_FILES' doc comment states the enumerate-don't-copy-wholesale purpose in the words the claim gives it. The over-report-never-under-report direction follows.

Both halves check out at source. `SNAPSHOT_FILES` is an explicit nine-entry enumeration whose doc states verbatim that it is "Enumerated rather than copied wholesale so that a future workspace file is a deliberate decision to ship or withhold" — a build predating an `acks.jsonl` entry never names the file and so never opens it, while still copying and reading `prose.jsonl`. And `snapshot::write`'s loop is `if src.exists() { fs::copy(...) }` with no removal pass, so a snapshot does retain a file the workspace no longer has.

The second half — "The writer must reconcile — deleting a snapshot file absent from the workspace — for the snapshot to mean 'the workspace at last render' rather than 'the most recent copy any build made of each file'" — does not say what the reconciliation enumerates, and the two available answers differ exactly on the cross-build case the claim's first half is about. `snapshot::write` (src/snapshot.rs:135-146) has only one enumeration in it, `for name in SNAPSHOT_FILES`, over a per-build `const [&str; 9]`, and never reads the snapshot directory. Reconciling over that constant leaves a tenth file a newer build wrote entirely unvisited by an older build's render, so the snapshot means "the workspace at last render, for the files the rendering build's manifest names, plus whatever any other build left behind" — which is the equality the claim says the fix establishes, and it is not established for the file this design adds. Reconciling over the snapshot directory instead does establish it, at the price of an older build deleting snapshot content it does not understand — a cost this memo never weighs, and a direct tension with `SNAPSHOT_FILES`' stated purpose that shipping or withholding a file be a deliberate per-build decision. Note the same residual hazard is what C14 cites to kill the withdrawal verb, so the two claims are consistent only under the manifest reading — under which this sentence's stated purpose is not achieved.

SNAPSHOT_FILES is an explicit nine-entry enumeration whose doc comment states the purpose the claim quotes ("a future workspace file is a deliberate decision to ship or withhold, not an accident of `cp -r`"); `write` iterates only that array, copies only `if src.exists()`, and contains no removal — so it accretes, and a build predating an `acks.jsonl` entry never visits the file. Reconciling over the manifest would indeed never visit an unnamed file, for the same reason.

The check side reads the snapshot's `prose.jsonl` by explicit name and computes the residue from it plus ledger claims and evidence records; nothing else in the snapshot feeds the finding, so a build predating the entry reads prose.jsonl unchanged and reproduces TET-30's un-suppressed listing.

"this needs two things rather than one" and "The writer must reconcile" hold only under a condition the claim does not state and that C14 removes: that the workspace's `acks.jsonl` can shrink. It cannot. `append_jsonl` opens with `.append(true)`, no production verb in src/ deletes a workspace log (all 21 `fs::remove*` matches are `#[cfg(test)]` scratch cleanup), and this design ships NO withdrawal verb (C14). So the workspace's ack log is monotone, and `snapshot::write`'s copy-only loop (src/snapshot.rs 135-146) can only leave the snapshot holding an EARLIER state of that log — a subset. A subset suppresses fewer blocks, i.e. over-reports, which is precisely the direction C4 declares acceptable. The under-reporting case the second leg exists to close — "a snapshot retains a log the workspace no longer has" — was reachable when an `Unack` event existed (it could invalidate an ack that the snapshot's stale copy still carried); once `Unack` is gone, reaching it requires an out-of-band act the memo does not name, such as deleting or restoring a workspace directory or re-rendering the memo from a different workspace, both of which also desynchronise `prose.jsonl` and `identity.json` and so surface through drift and grounding-provenance. This matters because C4 is an instruction to an implementer to change a shared, load-bearing writer, and C4 itself states the price: "a build reconciling over the directory deletes a snapshot file it does not understand". That price is general and permanent — every future snapshot file, including the TET-36 obligation ledger C19 plans to re-home these events into, becomes destroyable by any render from a build predating it, where today it would survive. The design pays a general, forward-facing destructive cost for a case its own no-withdrawal decision made unreachable through the tool. Either state the residual case reconciliation actually closes (and why it is worth that price), or narrow C4 to the manifest leg alone and drop `snapshot::write` from the modification targets.

Both load-bearing properties hold, but one supporting clause is false as written. Holds: SNAPSHOT_FILES (src/snapshot.rs:71) is an explicit `[&str; 9]` enumeration whose doc gives exactly the stated purpose ("a future workspace file is a deliberate decision to ship or withhold, not an accident of `cp -r`"), and `write` (snapshot.rs:135-146) only iterates it, so a build predating a tenth entry never opens the file and `write`'s body needs no change; `append_jsonl` (workspace.rs:451-456) is `create(true).append(true)` + `writeln!`, never truncating; no production code path deletes or truncates a workspace log. False as written: "none of it in the modules holding the authoring verbs" — the `fs::remove` sites are in review.rs, evidence.rs, facts.rs (559/576/589/599/601), workspace.rs and observe.rs, and facts.rs, observe.rs and workspace.rs are precisely the modules holding `fact`, `look`/`run` and `append_jsonl`. The removes are inside those modules' `#[cfg(test)]` regions, not absent from them, so the clause should say "in no production code path" rather than "in none of those modules". Secondarily, facts.rs:599 `remove_file(dir.join("refusals.log"))` is test *setup* (staging `a_snapshot_with_no_refusal_log_yields_no_windows`), not "scratch-directory teardown". Neither correction touches the monotonicity conclusion.

C4's conclusion "a snapshot's ack log, however stale, is a prefix of the workspace's: it holds a subset of the acks, suppresses a subset of the blocks, and therefore over-reports rather than under-reports" is refuted by construction on the workspace-identity axis, which neither of the claim's two premises addresses. The premises are about the ack log inside one workspace; the conclusion is about the snapshot's copy versus the workspace's, and the inference needs an unstated premise that a memo is only ever rendered from one workspace.

F2 witnesses that it is not: `render --out` (src/main.rs:826-858) takes its workspace from the free `--workspace` flag with nothing binding a memo path to a prior renderer, and `snapshot::write` (src/snapshot.rs:135-146) copies `for name in SNAPSHOT_FILES` under `if src.exists()` with no removal pass and no refusal, while re-minting and overwriting identity.json from whatever workspace it is handed. So: ack P in W1, `render --out M` (snapshot holds acks.jsonl=[Ack(P,k)]); later `--workspace W2 render --out M` where W2 has no acks.jsonl — a rebuilt state directory, a second machine, or a workspace reconstructed from the committed snapshot. The absent file is skipped rather than removed, the stale ack survives beside W2's prose and claims, and if P's text, cites and claim digests still match, P is suppressed with no acknowledgement anywhere in the rendering workspace. The snapshot's log is then a superset, not a prefix, and the direction is silent under-reporting. Nothing reddens: acks.jsonl is outside compose::render's inputs by C13's own choice, so drift cannot see it, and the log is well-formed so C11's unreadable disjunct does not fire.

This is one build, no mixed builds, no clock skew and no code path removing anything, so the revised premises do not close it. The withdrawn reconciliation pass was the only mechanism in the design that would have. Either restore a reconciliation (or a binding between a snapshot and the workspace identity that wrote it), or narrow C4 to the single-workspace case and propagate that narrowing into C16's cost argument and the "What changes, and what it costs" paragraph, which spend the unnarrowed one-directional guarantee.

Manifest, monotonicity and the identity gap all check out at the pin: SNAPSHOT_FILES is a nine-entry explicit enumeration whose doc comment states the ship-or-withhold purpose verbatim; snapshot::write copies present files and skips absent ones with no removal or reconciliation; --workspace is a free global clap flag with default_value "default" and the Render arm derives workspace_dir from it alone, never comparing against an existing <path>.tetel/. So a second workspace's render does leave a first workspace's acks.jsonl in place beside the second's prose/claims, while identity.json is overwritten — which is exactly the asymmetry the third (identity-equality) property closes.

Add `--level` to the refused set (and note that a shared `ProseRequest::Ack` variant cannot carry any of these refusals, since it has no field for the dropped inputs — each front end's chain must state them, which is the drift the shared shape was built to prevent).

Every asymmetry this claim names is in the source as written. mcp.rs:355 declares `text: String` with neither Option nor #[serde(default)] (every sibling optional field carries the attribute), so a missing text fails deserialisation before the handler's open_workspace/dispatch — no workspace::refuse is reached; main.rs's Command::Prose declares `text: Option<String>`, so the CLI does not. Both CLI text-consuming arms (Revise, Paragraph) call resolve_text_or_stdin(..., text.as_deref()), whose None case reads stdin, so a flagless ack would block — hence the positioning requirement. --level is indeed a separate CLI flag consumed only by the heading arm while ProseParams folds selector and value into one heading_level, so an enumeration written against the MCP shape would miss it; excluding --why, the other mode-bearing flags are exactly the six named. Both front ends select mode with an if/else-if chain building one variant and dropping fields it lacks (main.rs:782-809, mcp.rs:738-744), and prose.rs's own revise doc records the earlier instance of that defect (--cites "accepted alongside --revise and silently discarded"). Of the ack's refusals, exactly two pre-exist in prose::revise: the nonexistent-block refusal and `why.trim().is_empty()` backing "--revise requires --why (revisions must explain themselves)"; creation is ungated per the module doc, so heading/citation/claim-resolution gates are new.

The closing clause holds too: evidence records live at `<memo>.evidence.jsonl` beside the rendered memo (evidence.rs:415-421), never in the workspace directory, so an authoring verb genuinely has no evidence records in hand and cannot compute an anchor to decide whether a block is currently listed.

prop: An acknowledgement must not enter `render`'s output. Keeping the rendered bytes a function of facts, claims, prose, targets and transplants only — with `acks.jsonl` shipped by the snapshot copy loop but never read by `compose::render` — preserves the determinism the provenance-drift finding rests on, and buys a property that makes the required re-render honest rather than merely tolerable: re-rendering after an ack and nothing else rewrites the snapshot in place, since existing snapshot files are overwritten, while leaving the memo byte-identical. The discharge therefore shows up in version control as a change to the record and no change to the argument, which is exactly what it is.
note: The evidence supports that `snapshot::write` overwrites existing snapshot files, but it does not show that `acks.jsonl` is in `SNAPSHOT_FILES` or establish that `compose::render` never reads acknowledgements. Thus the claimed memo-byte identity and determinism after an ack are not demonstrated.

later.note: compose::render (compose.rs:79-94) reads exactly prose, claims, targets, transplants and facts and nothing else, so a log it never opens cannot enter the rendered bytes; snapshot::write copies each SNAPSHOT_FILES entry with "Existing files are overwritten" stated in its own doc comment, so a re-render after an ack rewrites the snapshot in place while producing byte-identical memo output.

`compose::render` reads exactly prose, claims, targets, transplants and facts and nothing else, so keeping `acks.jsonl` out of it leaves the rendered bytes unchanged; and `snapshot::write`'s doc states "Existing files are overwritten: re-rendering a memo replaces its snapshot" (F2), so a re-render after an ack rewrites the snapshot in place while producing a byte-identical memo.

prop: Supersession needs no verb and withdrawal needs one, and both are resolved by log order rather than by timestamp. Supersession is automatic: since suppression is existential over matching keys, a later ack with a different key simply fails to match and a duplicate ack for the same key changes nothing. Withdrawal is a second event, `Unack`, carrying a block id and its own required verbatim `--why`; suppression then requires a key-matching ack appended after the last `Unack` for that block. Naming only the block, rather than a key, is sufficient because a key-mismatched ack is already void. Resolving by position in an append-only log written one line per event, rather than by comparing timestamps, keeps the whole acknowledgement mechanism free of clock comparisons. Withdrawal has to exist: without it, an author who acknowledged in error and cannot yet rewrite the paragraph would have no honest act available — which is precisely the defect this design was written to remove, reproduced one level up.
note: The evidence shows that `ProseEvent` defines only `Create` and `Revise`, and querying a log containing `Ack` fails with “unknown variant `Ack`”; no `Unack` event or acknowledgement suppression logic is present.

later.note: `workspace::append_jsonl` writes exactly one line per event to an append-only file and `read_jsonl` returns them in file order, so "later than the last Unack" is decidable by position without any timestamp comparison — which is what the proposition rests on. Supersession-by-existential-match and the sufficiency of naming only the block follow from the key being an equality test that a mismatched ack simply fails.

"A duplicate ack for the same key changes nothing" is true of suppression and false of the output the design mandates. C8 puts only (block id, text, cite list, cited-claim digests) in the key; `--why` and the timestamp are recorded and unkeyed. Since every key component is fixed by the state the check recomputes, same-key duplicates are the only multiplicity reachable at suppression time — and C7 requires the collapsed bullet to carry, per acknowledged block, one acknowledgement timestamp and one `--why` verbatim. An author who acknowledges the same unchanged block twice with different reasons therefore leaves the report with two candidate reasons and two candidate timestamps and no stated rule for choosing, so two workspaces in identical states can print different bullets. The design needs one sentence — latest matching ack wins, or all matching acks print — and C14 currently reads as though the question does not arise.

The source facts are all correct: `snapshot::write` copies under `if src.exists()` and never removes, `SNAPSHOT_FILES` is an explicit enumeration so a build predating an acks entry refreshes prose.jsonl and claims.jsonl while never touching acks.jsonl, and the ack's other invalidators (block text, cite list, cited claim propositions) all travel in prose.jsonl and claims.jsonl, which every build ships and rewrites. The clause I cannot let stand as written is the reason given for removing `Unack`: "`snapshot::write` copies and never removes, so a snapshot's ack log is the most recent copy any build made of it rather than the workspace's log as of the last render." C4 of this same ledger states that this design **must** change exactly that — "The writer must reconcile — deleting a snapshot file absent from the workspace". Once C4's reconciliation lands, an appended `Unack` travels in the same rewritten acks.jsonl as every other ack and is no more droppable than they are for any current build; the asymmetry survives only via the *older-build* clause, which C14 also states but subordinates. So the proposition holds under a condition it does not state — that the reader is an older build — and its leading premise is one the memo elsewhere undertakes to falsify.

The mechanism the second consideration rests on is exact: `snapshot::write` iterates only SNAPSHOT_FILES, so a build predating an acks.jsonl entry refreshes prose.jsonl and claims.jsonl and leaves the ack log at whatever the last knowing render wrote — an Unack appended after that render never travels while the ack it cancelled, already in the snapshot, does. The clause about withdrawal having been designed in and then removed is about this memo's own drafting and is not settleable from source; nothing in the tree contradicts it.

The two source-anchored premises hold. Monotonicity: `append_jsonl` (workspace.rs:451-456) opens with `create(true).append(true)` and only writes a line, and no production code path in src/ removes or truncates a workspace log — every `fs::remove` is in a `#[cfg(test)]` region over a temp-dir scratch path. The `Unack` loss scenario is exactly what `snapshot::write` (snapshot.rs:135-146) implies: it copies only names in SNAPSHOT_FILES and never deletes, so a build predating the entry leaves a snapshot's ack log at whatever the last knowing render wrote — a later withdrawal would be invisible while the acknowledgement it cancelled survived. That a repaired paragraph voids its ack follows from the key including text and cite-list, which `prose_after_proof`'s own pair-keying (checks.rs:518-556) shows is the same quantity the trigger tracks. The rest — that matching is existential over keys, and the asymmetry argument for declining the verb — are design stipulations, coherent given those premises.

prop: This design knowingly breaks both halves of TET-30's C11 sentence "Nothing new ships in the snapshot, no schema changes": a tenth file ships, and a new event schema exists. The price is bounded and should be stated rather than absorbed. `check` always prints the binary that produced a report, on the stated ground that a report which does not name its build cannot be disbelieved, so two reports disagreeing about one memo's residue can be attributed to their checkers — which is sufficient for the only divergence this change can produce, an older build over-reporting an entry a newer one suppresses. It is not sufficient to tell the reader of a single old report that an acknowledgement exists at all; what covers that is the acknowledgement log itself, which the snapshot ships beside the memo and which is readable without any tetel build.
note: The evidence shows an added acknowledgement-log file in the snapshot and a corresponding event shape, deliberately departing from TET-30 C11. It also shows that reports include their producing build, while the plain acknowledgement log—not an old report alone—establishes that an acknowledgement exists.

later.note: The tetel-side halves are exact: `report::render` prints "checked by {build}" on every path including the no-rows path, its doc comment gives precisely the stated ground ("A report that does not name its build cannot be disbelieved", echoed in buildid.rs: "A verdict that names its checker can be disbelieved; one that does not, cannot"), and a jsonl log shipped in the snapshot is readable without any tetel build. What this pass could not establish is the attribution: a grep of docs/design/tet30-prose-revised-since-grounding.md confirms the sentence "Nothing new ships in the snapshot, no schema changes" occurs there exactly once, but I retrieved only the match count and did not open the surrounding text, so that the sentence belongs to that memo's C11 is unverified here.

`report::render`'s doc states the build "is *always* printed, including on the no-rows path, because the whole point is that two outputs which disagree can be told apart by their checker. A report that does not name its build cannot be disbelieved" — exactly the stated ground the proposition cites, and it covers attributing two divergent reports to their checkers without telling a single old report's reader that an ack exists. The tenth-file and new-schema price is real given SNAPSHOT_FILES is nine entries today (F2) and ProseEvent admits only Create/Revise (F3, F9).

C16's enumeration of cross-build divergence is incomplete, and the missing member is created by this memo's own C11. C16 asserts the build line is "sufficient for the only divergence this change can produce, an older build over-reporting an entry a newer one suppresses". C11 requires an unreadable acks.jsonl to redden by gaining a disjunct in machine_check_failed. Those two together produce a second divergence class the claim does not admit: on a snapshot whose acks.jsonl holds one malformed line, a build carrying the new disjunct exits 1 on the machine partition while a build predating the SNAPSHOT_FILES entry never opens the file and runs clean. F1 witnesses each step — src/lib.rs:132-211 names every snapshot input literally with no directory enumeration; src/snapshot.rs:185-205 shows snapshot::check only re-renders and imposes no completeness requirement; src/workspace.rs:459-471 shows read_jsonl returns Ok(empty) only for NotFound and Err for any parse failure or other IO error; src/report.rs:181-201 shows machine_check_failed gating the whole machine partition and the exit status. The corrupt state is reachable without any tooling, and the memo's own C17 line 3 and C21 concede a hand-edited snapshot ack log is invisible to drift, so nothing else reports it first.

What survives: "sufficient" — the build line does let a reader attribute a red/green disagreement as readily as an over-reported entry. What does not survive is "the only divergence". The condition C16 needs and does not state is that the snapshot's acks.jsonl is readable; outside it, the divergence is not an extra human-owed line but a build-dependent pass/fail, which the cost paragraph this claim backs ("What changes, and what it costs", cites C16/C8/C4) does not price. Either narrow the clause to divergences in the residue's human-owed entries and price the machine-partition one separately, or state that the ack log's readability is a precondition of the bounded-cost argument.

Both quoted grounds are verbatim. TET-30's C11 row (docs/design/tet30-prose-revised-since-grounding.md:104) does contain "Nothing new ships in the snapshot, no schema changes", so both halves are what this design breaks. report::render takes `build` and prints "checked by {build}" on the no-rows path and at the end of every normal report, with the doc comment stating exactly the ground the claim gives it — "A report that does not name its build cannot be disbelieved" — which is what lets either divergence be attributed to its checker while leaving the single-old-report reader uncovered.

The two divergence kinds are correctly typed. The ordinary one is human-owed: prose_revised_since_proof is a Findings field absent from machine_check_failed's explicit disjunction and from total_failures' sum, so an older build over-reporting one entry costs exactly one human-owed line. The sharper one is red-versus-green because SNAPSHOT_FILES is a closed nine-entry manifest, so a build predating the tenth entry never opens acks.jsonl and cannot reach any disjunct over it.

prop: Two entries are owed in `NON_COVERAGE`, by the list's own stated standard that a deliberate exclusion earns its own line because a refusal that fired is easily read as coverage it never claimed. First: that an acknowledgement records only that a human said they re-read the paragraph against its claims, and that nothing verifies the reading happened or judges whether the paragraph is faithful — the tool's silence after an ack is the author's assertion, not the tool's finding. Second: that an acknowledgement minted after the last `render --out` is not in the snapshot the check reads, so it does not suppress anything until the memo is re-rendered. Both are static general statements, which is the only form entries in this constant can take.
note: The evidence states that deliberate exclusions should have separate static lines and that passing checks do not settle human-owed matters, but it does not establish the specific acknowledgement semantics or the post-render snapshot behavior asserted here.

later.note: NON_COVERAGE's own comments state both halves of the standard invoked — "a refusal that fired is easily read as coverage it never claimed" and "A deliberate exclusion earns its own line, by the same standard as every other entry here" — and also state the form constraint: "This can only ever be the general statement — every string in this list is static and none is per-search". Both proposed entries are static general statements of that form, and the second is consistent with the check reading only the shipped snapshot.

The stated standard is in the constant verbatim: "Printed rather than left implicit, because a refusal that fired is easily read as coverage it never claimed", and "A deliberate exclusion earns its own line, by the same standard as every other entry here." The form constraint is also stated: "This can only ever be the general statement — every string in this list is static and none is per-search", and every element of `NON_COVERAGE` is indeed a `&'static str`. All three proposed entries are static general statements of that shape, and none duplicates an existing entry.

prop: Per-citation attribution is folded into the acknowledgement only as far as it honestly can be, which is not far. `NON_COVERAGE`'s last entry already states that whether a block's wording was ever examined against an earlier-settled co-citation is never answered by any listing, and the acknowledgement does not answer it either: the ack is per block, its key merely records every cited claim's digest, and the only place a per-citation judgement can appear is inside the author's verbatim `--why`, which the tool must not parse. The design's contribution is therefore to print the block's cited claim ids beside that verbatim reason in the acknowledged bullet, so a reader can pair the author's own words to the citations, and to leave the non-coverage entry standing.
note: The evidence supports the stated NON_COVERAGE limitation and shows the report printing each block's cited IDs beside the author's verbatim reason.
